Stacking combines different types of models with a meta-model; boosting usually combines many simple learners of one type, added in sequence.

examples.everyday: A good walk always boosts my energy, so I'm boosting my morning routine this month.
examples.professional: We're using gradient boosting on the churn data because it handles nonlinear interactions well.
examples.analytical: Boosting differs from bagging because each new learner is trained on the residual errors of the ensemble built so far.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay of tutors where each one only works on what the last one got wrong.
common_mistakes: Dropping the final t and saying BUS-ing, which sounds like a different word.
Using boosting as a general word for any model improvement in technical talk; it names a specific ensemble method.

conversation.text: Boosting trains weak learners in sequence, each focusing on the examples the previous ones got wrong.
AdaBoost was one of the first practical boosting algorithms.
Boosting morale on the team mattered as much as boosting accuracy.

senses.definition: Able to be spanned by, or as if by, a bridge.
Possible to reconcile.

core.definition: Able to be crossed or spanned, or, figuratively, able to be reconciled or overcome, as in differences or gaps.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, BRIDGE, and the -able ending has a lighter secondary stress. Say the dg as one sound, and avoid turning the ending into a separate word like able with a long a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests that a problem is solvable and that effort could close the gap.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in formal writing, analysis, or careful discussion of differences, rather than in casual speech. In everyday talk people often say 'we can work it out' or 'that's something we can fix.' If you use it, make sure the gap or difference is something that really can be closed.

distinctions.note: Reconcilable means able to be made consistent or brought into agreement, often for ideas or accounts, while bridgeable suggests closing a gap or distance between two separate sides.
Surmountable means able to be overcome or climbed over, usually for obstacles, while bridgeable focuses on connecting across a divide.

examples.everyday: The gap between our two schedules seems bridgeable if we meet halfway on Thursday.
examples.professional: The mismatch between the two data sources looks bridgeable with a simple mapping table and a few validation checks.
examples.analytical: Whether the divide between faith and reason is bridgeable depends on how we define each term and what counts as evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a river narrow enough for a footbridge, a bridgeable gap is one that a connection can actually span.
nuance.etymology: From bridge (Old English brycg) plus the suffix -able, meaning able to be.
common_mistakes: Spelling it bridgable, which is less standard than bridgeable in American writing.
Using it only for physical distances, when it is often used figuratively for differences.
Confusing it with bridged, the past tense or past participle of bridge.

senses.definition: Title of respect for an adult male member of a religious or fraternal order.
senses.example: At the monastery, Brother Stephen supervises the kitchen.

senses.definition: Title of respect for an adult male member of a fraternal/sororal organization, or comrade in a movement, or even a stranger using fictive kin.
senses.example: Brother Thomas welcomed the new members to the lodge with a firm handshake.

senses.definition: A title used to personify or respectfully refer to concepts or animals.
senses.example: The Native American had a kinship with nature, even referring to Mother Earth and Brother Bear.

core.definition: A title of respect for a man who belongs to a religious community, or a male fellow member of a group.

pronunciation.tip: The th is voiced, as in 'they', and the final -er is a weak, rhotic vowel. Stress the first syllable only.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies closeness, loyalty and respect, though in religious settings it can sound formal.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, brother usually means a male sibling, and speakers casually call close male friends 'brother' too. In church or monastic settings, it is a formal title of respect for a religious man who is not a priest. Americans also use it in phrases like 'brother in Christ' and as a slang greeting among friends.

distinctions.note: Sibling is a neutral term for a brother or sister, while brother is specific to male siblings and can carry religious or fraternal meanings.
Brethren is an old plural form used mainly in religious or formal language; everyday Americans say brothers.

examples.everyday: My older brother drove up from Atlanta to help us move this weekend.
examples.professional: The parish office asked for a brother from the community to help lead the Tuesday study group.
examples.analytical: In the New Testament, brother is used both for kinship and for the bond within the church, so the term carries a relational meaning that goes beyond blood.

nuance.analogy: A brother title is like a family name given to members of a larger household, so that people who were not born into the family still share its name.
nuance.etymology: From Old English brōthor, related to Latin frater and Greek phrater, meaning a male sibling or member of the same group.
common_mistakes: Using brother for a male cousin or in-law without saying brother-in-law or cousin.
Mispronouncing the th as an unvoiced sound like 'thin'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is 'ach (אָח), meaning brother, relative or kinsman, and the Greek word is adelphos (ἀδελφός), meaning brother, a male sibling or fellow believer. In Genesis 4:9 (RSV), Cain's question after killing Abel, Am I my brother's keeper?, shows that brotherhood implies moral responsibility. In Matthew 12:50, Jesus says that whoever does the will of his Father in heaven is his brother, sister and mother, widening the meaning of family to include obedient disciples. In Romans 8:29, Paul calls Christ the firstborn among many brethren, meaning that believers share a family relation to him.

traditions.view: Monks and nuns are often addressed as brother or sister as a sign of humility and shared commitment, and the title is used within monastic communities rather than as a clerical rank.
A religious brother is a man who professes vows in a religious institute but is not ordained a priest, and the title differs from a priest's title of Father.

Protestants use brother for fellow believers in the church, and some groups such as the Moravians and Brethren use it as a formal term for members, while other churches use it mainly in informal address.

senses.definition: A rabbit, especially a juvenile one.
A bunny girl: a nightclub waitress who wears a costume having rabbit ears and tail.
senses.example: The 1960s-style club hired a bunny to carry drinks in rabbit ears and a tail.

senses.definition: Synonym of rabbit (“batsman frequently dismissed by the same bowler”).
senses.example: The batsman was a bunny for that bowler, getting out to him every single match.

senses.definition: A sudden enlargement or mass of ore, as opposed to a vein or lode.
senses.example: Miners struck a bunny of rich ore that far exceeded what the vein had promised.

senses.definition: In basketball, an easy shot (i.e. one right next to the bucket) that is missed.
senses.example: He lost the game when he missed a bunny right under the basket in overtime.

senses.definition: (dated) A menstrual pad.
senses.example: My grandmother still called sanitary pads bunnies, a term from her youth.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Easy or unchallenging.
senses.example: Let’s start on the bunny slope.

senses.definition: Resembling a bun (small bread roll).
senses.example: The dough came out soft and bunny, rising into little rolls that looked like buns.

core.definition: A rabbit, especially a young or small one; a cute, informal name for a rabbit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, BUH-nee. The first vowel is short and relaxed like 'uh', not the 'oo' of 'boon', and the second syllable is a light 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and affectionate. It suggests small, soft, cute animals, and it can sound childish when used for an adult's wild rabbit.
nuance.usage_note: Bunny is the everyday word for a rabbit when you talk to children or about a pet, and Americans say it naturally for the Easter Bunny. For a wild rabbit in a serious discussion, rabbit is more neutral. In basketball slang, a bunny is an easy shot right next to the basket, and as an adjective it means easy, as in a bunny shot or a bunny ball.

distinctions.note: Rabbit is the neutral word for the animal, while bunny is cuter and mostly used for small, young, or pet rabbits.
Hares are larger, with longer ears and legs, and they are born with fur and open eyes; they are not rabbits.

examples.everyday: Look at that little bunny hopping across the yard!
examples.professional: Our veterinary clinic sees so many pet bunnies that we added a separate exam room for them.
examples.analytical: Calling a wild rabbit a bunny softens the animal in the mind, which can shape how people think about its welfare.

nuance.analogy: A bunny is the rabbit you would want to hold, while a rabbit is the one you would find in a field.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; the -y ending is an English diminutive, and the root may be a dialect word for a rabbit.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it BOO-nee, as in 'boon', instead of BUH-nee
Using bunny for an adult wild rabbit in formal writing, where it sounds childish

senses.definition: Busy; full of energy and noisy activity.
senses.example: bustling marketplace

senses.definition: A bustle; a busy stir.
senses.example: the bustlings of waiters in the crowded restaurant

core.definition: Full of busy, energetic activity and noise, especially describing a place such as a street, market, or city.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is often reduced so the word sounds like BUHS-ling, with the l as a syllabic sound and no clear 'tel' or 'tuh' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, suggesting lively energy. It can imply noise and crowding, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bustling most often for places: a bustling downtown, a bustling kitchen, a bustling airport. It is a friendly way to describe a lively scene without criticizing it. The noun 'bustle' is also used, but mainly in phrases like 'the bustle of the city.'

distinctions.note: Busy describes a person, schedule, or place with much to do; bustling emphasizes noise, movement, and energy in a public space.
Crowded focuses on too many people in a space; bustling adds the sense of active, lively movement.
Hectic suggests stress and disorder, while bustling is usually neutral or positive.

examples.everyday: Times Square is always bustling on Friday nights, so we usually take the subway instead.
examples.professional: The open-plan office was bustling with the sales team before the quarterly launch.
examples.analytical: Jane Jacobs's account of bustling city sidewalks argues that everyday street life helps create public safety.

nuance.analogy: Like a beehive on a warm day: full of purposeful movement and a steady hum.
nuance.etymology: Present participle of the verb bustle, whose origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
Using bustling for a single busy person; it is mainly used for places and scenes.

senses.definition: An outgoing telephone call.
senses.example: I made a callout to my sister in Denver before the flight boarded.

senses.definition: An instance of being summoned to visit a certain place in order to provide assistance; an instance of summoning someone who is on call.
senses.example: I had to pay for the callout of the plumber after the pipe burst.

senses.definition: A meeting or rally held in order to find interested participants, e.g. for an activity or sports team.
senses.example: So many people attended the basketball callout that the coach decided to form two teams.

senses.definition: An invitation to fight.
senses.example: The rapper's latest song was a callout aimed at a rival from Atlanta.

senses.definition: A request for people to join or take part.
senses.example: The town posted a callout for volunteers to help clear debris after the storm.

senses.definition: A pull quote: an excerpt from an article (such as in a news magazine) that is duplicated in a large font alongside the article so as to grab a reader's attention and indicate the article's topic.
senses.example: The magazine ran a callout in large type quoting the reporter's line about the budget.

senses.definition: An annotation that pertains to a specific location in a body of text or a graphic, and that is visually linked to that location by a mark or a matching pair of marks.
senses.example: In the diagram, each part has a callout with a line pointing to the exact component.

senses.definition: The act of calling out from work, i.e. announcing that one cannot attend; the act of calling in sick.
senses.example: He texted a callout to his manager at six, saying his fever was too high.

senses.definition: A form of verbal abuse with the intention of making the victim feel guilty.
senses.example: Her mother's constant callout about never visiting left him feeling guilty all week.

senses.definition: The invocation of an external third-party component.
senses.example: The build failed because the callout to the payment library timed out.

senses.definition: A scheduled appointment for which a prisoner may go somewhere.
senses.example: The inmate had a callout to the prison dentist scheduled for Tuesday morning.

core.definition: A summons sent to responders such as police, firefighters, or technicians to deal with an emergency or urgent problem.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable in this noun, unlike the verb call out, where out gets the stress. Keep the ow diphthong clear, as in how or out.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in emergency services, where it describes a routine dispatch. It can be negative when used for public criticism of someone online.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use callout for emergency and service calls, such as a fire department callout or a technician's after-hours callout. In online culture, a public callout is a post that publicly criticizes someone's behavior, and it can be harsh. Remember that the noun is one word and the verb is two words: call out.

distinctions.note: Dispatch is the act of sending help or the person who sends it, while a callout is the summons itself.
A shout-out is public praise or recognition, while a callout is usually a summons or public criticism.

examples.everyday: Dad got a callout to the plant at midnight again, so he was exhausted all weekend.
examples.professional: The on-call engineer received a callout for a database outage at 2 a.m. and fixed it within the hour.
examples.analytical: A public callout can enforce accountability, yet it also tends to reduce complex disputes to a single damning post.

nuance.analogy: A callout is like a fire alarm: a sudden signal that demands an immediate response from those on duty.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the phrasal verb call out, to summon or announce, as a compound noun.
common_mistakes: Writing the noun as two words, call out, when it should be callout.
Stressing the second word in the noun, instead of the first.

senses.definition: To give birth to a calf.
senses.example: The farmer could tell Bessie was about to calve.

senses.definition: To assist in a cow’s giving birth to a calf.
senses.example: The farmer calved Bessie for almost two hours.

senses.definition: To give birth to (a calf).
To shed a large piece.
senses.example: The glacier was starting to calve even as we watched.

senses.definition: To break off.
senses.example: The sea was dangerous because of icebergs calving off the nearby glacier.

senses.definition: To shed (a large piece); to set loose (a mass of ice).
senses.example: The glacier was starting to calve an iceberg even as we watched.

core.definition: To give birth to a calf, or to help a cow give birth to its calf.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short 'a' like 'cat'. Do not add a vowel after the v, and do not pronounce the final e, which is silent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a farming and ranching term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use calve mostly in agriculture, ranching, and rural contexts. In everyday speech many people say 'have a calf' or 'give birth'. The word also appears in the phrase 'the glacier calved' for ice breaking off a glacier, which is common in American geography and news about Alaska.

distinctions.note: Give birth is general and is used for people and animals; calve is used only for cows, and other large animals in some contexts.
When ice breaks off a glacier, the same verb is used, so context matters: a rancher and a glaciologist use it differently.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's cow calved last night, so we went out early to check on her.
examples.professional: The ranch manager said the herd would start to calve in late March.
examples.analytical: The verb calve, applied to a glacier, describes ice breaking away from the ice front rather than biological birth.

nuance.analogy: Calve works like a dam giving way: a large piece breaks off from something bigger.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cealfian, from calf.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as kalv, adding a sound after the v.
Using calve for other animals in ordinary speech; it is mainly for cows.

calve.etymology: From Middle English *calven*, from Old English **calfian*, *cealfian*, from **kalbōn*, from Proto-Germanic **kalbōną* (“to calve”), from **kalbaz* (“calf”).

senses.definition: A device for taking still or moving pictures or photographs.
The viewpoint in a three-dimensional game or simulation.
senses.example: Switching the camera to first-person view made the narrow corridors much easier to navigate.

senses.definition: A vaulted room.
senses.example: Pilgrims gathered beneath the vaulted camera, its ceiling painted with faded gold stars.

senses.definition: A judge's private chamber, where cases may be heard in camera.
senses.example: The judge ordered the testimony heard in camera to protect the identity of the informant.

core.definition: A device for taking still photographs or moving pictures, or the equipment that records images for film or video.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The word has three syllables, but fast American speech often squeezes the middle schwa so it sounds like 'KAM-ruh'. The final r is flapped or light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names an object and has no emotional charge, though phrases like 'on camera' can imply public exposure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'take a picture' or 'take a photo' rather than 'make a photo', and they often say 'camera' for a phone camera. In video calls, people say 'turn on your camera' or 'camera on, please.' The phrase 'in camera' means in private, usually in legal or formal contexts.

distinctions.note: A camcorder is a portable device designed for video, while a camera can take still pictures, video, or both.
A webcam is a small camera attached to a computer, mainly for video calls, while a camera is any device that records images.

examples.everyday: Can you take a picture of us with my camera? Stand over by the tree so the lighting is better.
examples.professional: Please turn your camera on during the meeting so the team can see you when we review the design.
examples.analytical: The camera obscura projected an image onto a surface through a small hole, anticipating the optical principles of the modern camera.

nuance.analogy: A camera is like a box with a tiny window that catches light and freezes it onto a surface.
nuance.etymology: From Latin camera, vaulted room or chamber, from Greek kamara, meaning vault.
common_mistakes: Saying 'make a photo' instead of 'take a picture' or 'take a photo'
Stressing the middle syllable as in 'kuh-MER-uh'

camera.etymology: Latin *camera* (“chamber or bedchamber”), from Ancient Greek *καμάρα* (“anything with an arched cover, a covered carriage or boat, a vaulted chamber, a vault”), of origin, from **kamarā-* (“something curved”), from **kamárati*, from **kmárati*, ultimately…

senses.definition: A pattern on clothing consisting of irregularly shaped patches that are either greenish/brownish, brownish/whitish, or bluish/whitish, as used by ground combat forces.
senses.example: He wore a green and brown camo jacket for the early morning deer hunt.

senses.definition: Clothes made from camouflage fabric, for concealment in combat or hunting.
senses.example: Hunters often wear camo in the woods so that the deer cannot spot them.

senses.definition: Clipping of camouflage.
senses.example: My brother just calls it camo, not camouflage, when he talks about his jacket.

senses.definition: To camouflage.
senses.example: The crew camoed the truck with branches and netting before the patrol left.

senses.definition: To put on camouflage clothing.
senses.example: Before the dawn hunt, he camoed up in the dark, pulling on his patterned gear.

core.definition: Clothing or fabric with a mottled pattern of green, brown, gray, or tan, designed to help people blend in with their surroundings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final vowel is a long 'oh', not 'oo'. Do not stress the second syllable as in the full word 'camouflage', which stresses -flahzh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds casual and practical, and it is commonly used in hunting and military contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use camo in casual speech for clothing, gear, or patterns, such as 'camo pants' or 'a camo hat.' For formal writing, they use camouflage. As a verb, to camo is rare, so say 'to camouflage' instead.

distinctions.note: Camouflage is the formal, general term for concealment by any means, while camo is the informal name for the patterned clothing.
A disguise changes how a person looks to hide their identity, while camo is a pattern that helps them blend into nature.

examples.everyday: He wears his camo pants every time he goes deer hunting, even when it's not very cold.
examples.professional: Procurement ordered new desert camo uniforms for the training unit, which will arrive next quarter.
examples.analytical: The pattern of modern military camo reflects research on how the eye detects edges, shapes, and contrast.

nuance.analogy: Camo works like a leaf in the forest: it is hard to see because it looks like the surroundings.
nuance.etymology: Clipped from camouflage, from French camouflage, from camoufler, to disguise, from Italian camuffare.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing camo as 'kah-MOO' with stress on the second syllable
Misspelling camouflage as 'camoflage' by dropping the u

senses.definition: Funds that are spent by a company to acquire or upgrade a long-term asset.

core.definition: Money a company spends to buy, build, or upgrade long-term assets such as buildings, equipment, or software.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on PEN in expenditure, and capital keeps a lighter secondary stress. The t in capital is a quick flap that sounds almost like a d, and -ture is pronounced 'cher'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a spending decision; it sounds positive when it signals growth and negative when it drains cash.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in finance meetings, budget reviews, and annual reports. It is often shortened to capex, pronounced KAY-pecks. Everyday costs such as rent and salaries are called operating expenses, or opex, not capital expenditure.

distinctions.note: Operating expenses are day-to-day costs like rent and salaries; capital expenditure buys assets that last for years.
Investment is broader and can mean buying stocks; capital expenditure specifically means spending on a company's long-term physical or digital assets.

examples.everyday: Our company is holding off on big purchases this year, so there is no new equipment in the budget.
examples.professional: Finance wants the capital expenditure forecast for the data center by Friday so we can plan the hardware refresh.
examples.analytical: Economists separate capital expenditure from current spending because the former creates assets whose returns extend across many future periods.

nuance.analogy: Capital expenditure is like buying a car rather than buying gas: the car is a long-term asset you will use for years.
nuance.etymology: Capital from Latin capitalis, of the head, and expenditure from Latin expendere, to weigh out or spend.
common_mistakes: Confusing capital here with money in general or with a city; in this term it means long-term assets.
Using the term for daily costs; those are operating expenses.

senses.definition: That captivates; fascinating.
senses.example: Her lecture on Augustine's confessions was captivating from the first sentence onward.

senses.definition: Very beautiful or attractive.
senses.example: The autumn sunset over the lake was captivating, and everyone stopped to take photos.

core.definition: So interesting, charming, or attractive that it holds your complete attention.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAP. The final '-ing' is a light 'ing' sound, and the middle vowel is reduced to 'tih', so avoid saying 'ting' with a hard 't' ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something as charming, engaging, or beautiful, and is often used for people, stories, or performances.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'captivating' to praise a speaker, a book, a view, or a person's smile. In casual speech, people often say 'really interesting' or 'so cool', so this word sounds slightly polished. It is a safe choice in reviews, introductions, and descriptions.

distinctions.note: 'Interesting' is a general, mild word, while 'captivating' signals a much stronger, almost absorbing appeal.
'Beautiful' describes looks, while 'captivating' can describe charm, personality, or a story that holds your attention.

examples.everyday: That new podcast is captivating, so I listened to the whole thing on my drive to work.
examples.professional: She gave a captivating presentation on our churn data that got everyone asking follow-up questions.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of memory is captivating because it reveals the self as both mystery and witness.

nuance.analogy: A captivating story is like a good campfire: it draws everyone in and keeps them sitting still.
nuance.etymology: From 'captivate' (from Late Latin 'captivare', to take captive), with the English participle ending '-ing'.
common_mistakes: Using 'captivating' to describe how you feel; say 'I am captivated' instead.
Confusing it with 'captive', which means held prisoner.
Stressing the wrong syllable in pronunciation.

senses.definition: Insurance against damages to, or theft of, a car.

core.definition: Insurance that pays for damage to or theft of your car, and often for injuries or damage you cause to others.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'car', with a lighter stress on 'shur' in 'insurance'. Avoid stressing the first syllable of 'insurance', and keep the 'r' sounds clear in both words.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday term for a required or important expense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'car insurance' most often in daily conversation, and 'auto insurance' is also common, especially in insurance ads and paperwork. Most states require drivers to carry at least liability coverage, so people talk about it often. A natural reply to 'Do you have car insurance?' is 'Yes, with a company near my house'.

distinctions.note: In American usage the two terms mean essentially the same thing, though 'auto insurance' sounds slightly more formal or industry-oriented.
'Health insurance' covers medical costs, while 'car insurance' covers vehicles and some liability for accidents.

examples.everyday: My car insurance went up again this year, so I'm going to shop around for a better rate.
examples.professional: Our fleet team checked the car insurance policies for the company vehicles before approving the new routes.
examples.analytical: Car insurance markets reveal how risk is priced, since premiums reflect driving records, location, and the likelihood of claims.

nuance.analogy: Car insurance is like a safety net under a trapeze artist: you hope you never need it, but it catches you when something goes wrong.
nuance.etymology: 'Car' is from Latin 'carrus', and 'insurance' is from Old French 'enseurer' (to make secure), from Latin roots meaning to make sure.
common_mistakes: Using 'a car insurance' with an article, since the term is uncountable in general use; say 'car insurance' or 'a car insurance policy'.
Confusing it with 'car registration', which is a government requirement, not insurance.
Stressing 'in' in 'insurance' too strongly, as in 'in-SUR-ance' with the wrong vowel.

conversation.text: My car insurance went up after that fender bender last year.
You have to have car insurance to drive legally in almost every state.
Does your car insurance cover rental cars, or should I buy theirs?

senses.definition: Containing or producing carbon.
senses.example: The chemist reported that the sample was highly carboniferous, containing nearly forty percent carbon by mass.

core.definition: Relating to the geological period about 359 to 299 million years ago, when many coal deposits formed; producing coal.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, NIF, and the -er- is a light, reduced r-colored vowel, not a full 'air' sound. Don't put the stress on the first syllable or pronounce it as separate 'carbon' and 'iferous' words.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term and is almost never used in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in geology, paleontology, textbooks and museum exhibits, often as the proper name 'the Carboniferous period' with a capital C. In casual conversation, people would just say 'the coal-forming era' or 'the age of coal swamps'. Use it in writing when you need the exact geological term.

distinctions.note: Carbonaceous means made of or containing carbon, a broad chemistry term, while carboniferous specifically refers to the geological period or to rocks and deposits that produced coal.

examples.everyday: My son got really into dinosaurs, and now he wants to know everything about the Carboniferous period.
examples.professional: The core samples show a sharp change in pollen types that marks the transition out of the Carboniferous strata.
examples.analytical: Most of the world's large coal reserves were laid down in the Carboniferous, when vast swamp forests were buried and compressed over millions of years.

nuance.analogy: Think of the Carboniferous as the planet's great coal factory, the era when swamp plants piled up and turned into the coal we still mine.
nuance.etymology: From Latin carbo (coal) and -ferous (bearing), meaning coal-bearing.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in CAR-bo-NIF-er-us; the main stress is on NIF.
Using it to mean 'containing carbon' in general chemistry; in everyday technical writing the geological sense is the one meant.

senses.definition: Close attention; concern; responsibility.
senses.example: Care should be taken when holding babies.

senses.definition: Worry.
senses.example: I don’t have a care in the world.

senses.definition: Maintenance, upkeep.
senses.example: dental care

senses.definition: The treatment of those in need (especially as a profession).
The object of watchful attention or anxiety.
To be concerned (about), to have an interest (in); to feel concern (about).
senses.example: She doesn’t care what you think.

senses.definition: To want, to desire; to like; to be inclined towards or interested in.
senses.example: Would you care for another slice of cake?

senses.definition: To be affected by, to treat as relevant for a subsequent course of action.
(with for) To look after or look out for.
senses.example: Young children can learn to care for a pet.

senses.definition: To mind; to object.

core.definition: Close attention, concern, and responsibility for someone or something, shown through what you do.

pronunciation.tip: Use one clear vowel and finish with a relaxed r. Don't turn it into a long 'ay' sound. American speakers pronounce the r, unlike many British speakers who drop it.

nuance.connotation: Positive, because it signals kindness, responsibility, and attentiveness. It turns negative mainly in phrases like 'I don't care', which can sound dismissive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say take care of for looking after someone or something, and use health care or child care for services. In casual speech, 'I don't care' can sound rude, so soften it with 'I don't mind' or 'whatever works for you'. 'Would you care for some coffee?' is a polite offer, common when hosting or in restaurants.

distinctions.note: Worry is anxious thinking about something bad that might happen, while care is active concern or responsibility for someone or something.
Attention is mental focus in the moment, while care includes ongoing concern for someone's or something's wellbeing.

examples.everyday: Thanks for watching the kids last night; we really appreciate the care you showed them.
examples.professional: Please take care when you update the production database, since one mistake could affect every customer.
examples.analytical: Feminist ethicists have argued that care, not only rules, is the foundation of moral responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Care is like tending a garden: it needs regular attention, not just one good day of work.
nuance.etymology: From Old English caru, meaning sorrow or grief; the sense of attentive concern developed later.
common_mistakes: Saying 'care about' when you mean 'take care of', as in 'I'll care about the children' instead of 'I'll take care of the children'.
Using a flat 'I don't care' with a friend, which can sound cold or rude in American conversation.

care.etymology: From Middle English *care*, from Old English *caru*, *ċearu* (“care, concern, anxiety, sorrow, grief, trouble”), from **karu*, from Proto-Germanic **karō* (“care, sorrow, cry”), from Proto-Indo-European **ǵeh₂r-* (“shout, call”).

senses.definition: An act of endearment; any act or expression of affection; an embracing, or touching, with tenderness.
senses.example: A gentle caress of her cheek told him everything she could not say aloud.

senses.definition: A gentle stroking or rubbing.
To touch or kiss lovingly; to fondle.
senses.example: She loves being caressed by her boyfriend.

senses.definition: To affect as if with a caress.
senses.example: The evening breeze seemed to caress the tall grass along the riverbank.

core.definition: A gentle touch, stroke, or kiss that shows love or affection; to touch someone gently with love.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. The first vowel is a reduced 'uh' sound, and the final 's' is a clear, unvoiced 's' like 'ss'. Non-native speakers sometimes stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive and tender. It suggests love, comfort, or gentleness, and it can sound romantic or poetic in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use caress mainly in writing, poetry, or romantic and emotional descriptions, such as 'a gentle caress on her cheek.' In everyday speech, people more often say 'touch,' 'stroke,' or 'hug.' Using caress for a casual pat on the shoulder would sound too intense or literary.

distinctions.note: Touch is a neutral, general word for contact, while caress specifically suggests tender, affectionate contact.
Stroke suggests a slow, repeated movement across a surface, often used for hair, a pet, or a cheek; caress has more emotional tone.
Embrace means to hold someone in your arms, while caress is about gentle touching, usually with the hands.

examples.everyday: She gave his hand a gentle caress before she left for work.
examples.professional: The brand's campaign has a soft, caress-like tone that feels too sentimental for a bank.
examples.analytical: The poem is a caress of sound, with each line softening the one before until the final image feels like a touch.

nuance.analogy: A caress is like a warm blanket laid gently over someone: the touch is soft, deliberate, and meant to comfort rather than to grip.
nuance.etymology: From French caresse, from Italian carezza, from Latin carus, meaning dear.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (KAR-ess).
Using caress for any touch, when it suggests tenderness and affection.
Using caress in casual speech where touch or hug would be more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV does not use caress often. The nearest Hebrew idea is metsachaq, a word for playing, laughing, or fondling, which appears in Genesis 26:8 when Isaac is seen fondling Rebekah his wife. This shows that the Bible treats affectionate touch within marriage as a sign of intimacy. Song of Songs 2:6 describes a lover's embrace with a left hand under the head and a right hand embracing, which is the same tender affection described by caress.

caress.etymology: From French *caresse*, from Italian *carezza* (“dear”), from Latin *cārus* (“dear”), from Proto-Indo-European **keh₂-*, akin to.

senses.definition: The act of cartelizing.

core.definition: The process of organizing an industry or market into a cartel, so that producers coordinate their prices and output.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'zay', and the earlier syllables are reduced to a schwa. Pronounce the 'ti' ending as 'shun', and keep the r clear in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most economic and legal contexts, because it describes organized price-fixing or market control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cartelization in economics, antitrust and policy discussions, usually in academic or regulatory writing. It is a technical word and rarely appears in casual talk. In everyday speech, people say that an industry colluded or fixed prices.

distinctions.note: Collusion is the general act of secretly cooperating to gain an unfair advantage, while cartelization describes the process of forming an organized cartel.
Consolidation means merging companies into fewer firms, while cartelization means coordinating separate firms to control prices or output.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says the egg prices went up together because of some kind of cartelization, but I'm not sure that's true.
examples.professional: The compliance team flagged signs of cartelization in the bidding data, so legal wants a full review before we renew the contracts.
examples.analytical: Economists disagree about whether cartelization is easier in industries with few firms and transparent prices, and the empirical evidence is mixed.

nuance.analogy: Like a group of separate runners who agree to slow down together so none of them has to race.
common_mistakes: Confusing cartelization with consolidation, which is merging companies rather than coordinating them.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the 'zay' syllable.

senses.definition: To make into a castle: to build in the form of a castle or to add battlements to an existing building.
(rare) To take the form of a castle.
senses.example: The clouds began to castellate along the horizon, forming battlement-like towers.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) Castle-like: built or shaped like a castle.
senses.example: The sandstone cliffs stood castellate above the river, their rounded towers catching the light.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) Castled: having or furnished with castles.
senses.example: The Rhineland valley is castellate, with a fortified ruin on nearly every hilltop.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) Housed or kept in a castle.
senses.example: The ancient family archives remained castellate in the stone keep for generations.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To build or fit a structure with battlements or other castle-style features, so that it looks like a castle or small fortress.

pronunciation.tip: The corrected stress falls on the first syllable, and the first vowel is a short a as in cat, not cot. The final -late is a clear long a, not a reduced vowel. The given /ˈkastələt/ is replaced with the verb form Americans use.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a building feature without judging it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use castellate mainly in architecture, historic preservation, and history writing, to describe buildings with battlements or castle-like outlines. In everyday talk, people say add battlements or make it look like a castle. Its adjective form, castellated, is more common than the verb.

distinctions.note: Crenellate specifically means to add battlements with notches, while castellate can mean to give a building castle-like character more broadly.
Castle is the noun for the building, whereas castellate is the verb meaning to make a building into a castle or give it castle features.

examples.everyday: Whoever designed that house castellated the roof, which is why it looks like a little fort.
examples.professional: The preservation board reviewed plans to castellate the warehouse facade for the new hotel.
examples.analytical: Medieval builders often castellated manor houses not only for defense but also to signal rank and legal privilege.

nuance.analogy: Like icing a plain cake with a crown of peaks: the form is decorative, but it announces what kind of building it is.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin castellatus, from Latin castellum, 'small fortress,' with the verb suffix -ate.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel like the a in father, instead of the short a in cat.
Using castellate as a noun; the noun form is castellation.

castellate.etymology: From Medieval Latin *castellātus* (“fortified” “made into a castle”), from *castellum* + *-ātus*.

senses.definition: To accelerate a process.
To inspire significantly by catalysis.
senses.example: The grant money catalyzed a surge of new research into renewable battery chemistry.

senses.definition: To bring about the catalysis of a chemical reaction.

core.definition: To cause or speed up a process or change, or to bring about a chemical reaction by acting as a catalyst.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAT, and the final syllable rhymes with 'prize.' Do not pronounce the middle syllable as 'uh-LYZE' with stress on it.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it usually describes speeding up or enabling progress.
nuance.usage_note: In American English the spelling is 'catalyze,' while British writers use 'catalyse.' Americans use it in business and science contexts, like 'the merger will catalyze growth.' In casual speech, people often say 'spark' or 'kick off' instead.

distinctions.note: Spark is informal and suggests starting something suddenly; catalyze suggests speeding up a change that is already underway.
Accelerate means to speed up in general; catalyze implies a specific agent or event that makes the change happen faster.

examples.everyday: That new coffee shop on our street really catalyzed the whole neighborhood's social life.
examples.professional: We hope the pilot program will catalyze adoption of the new analytics platform across the company.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the printing press did not merely record ideas but catalyzed a new public sphere.

nuance.analogy: Like a spark plug in an engine: it does not supply the power, but without it the fuel never ignites.
nuance.etymology: From catalysis, from Greek katalysis 'dissolution,' with the verb suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling catalyse in American writing.
Using catalyze for a change that is slow and gradual; it implies a quicker acceleration.

senses.definition: A symmetric continuous probability distribution with fat tails, with probability density function that is.

core.definition: A symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution with very heavy tails, so its mean and variance are undefined.

pronunciation.tip: Americans usually say Cauchy as KOH-shee, not the French ko-SHEE or the spelling-based KAW-chee. The main stress in distribution falls on -BYOO-, so keep the first syllables light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in statistics and probability.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and statisticians use this term when they need a distribution with heavy tails, such as when modeling outliers or testing robustness. Americans also say 'Lorentzian' in physics for the same shape, and a Cauchy with one degree of freedom is the same as a Student's t distribution. Do not use it casually to mean any unusual distribution.

distinctions.note: A normal distribution has thin tails and finite mean and variance, while a Cauchy distribution has heavy tails and no defined mean or variance.
A Student's t-distribution with one degree of freedom is exactly a Cauchy distribution, so the two terms name the same shape in that case.

examples.everyday: I told my friend the sample average kept jumping around, and he asked if we were dealing with a Cauchy distribution.
examples.professional: The fraud model's residuals looked heavy-tailed, so we tested a Cauchy distribution to check how robust our estimates were.
examples.analytical: Because the Cauchy distribution has no finite expected value, the law of large numbers does not apply to the sample average.

nuance.analogy: Like a bowling alley where most balls hit the pins but a few land in another county, a Cauchy sample sometimes produces wild values that never settle down.
nuance.etymology: Named after the French mathematician Augustin-Louis Cauchy, 1789 to 1857.
common_mistakes: Assuming the distribution has a mean or variance, since it does not.
Pronouncing Cauchy as KAW-chee, which is not the common American pronunciation.

senses.definition: In a cavalier manner.

core.definition: In a careless, dismissive way that shows little concern for something important.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the third syllable, 'LEER', with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. The ending is a clear 'lee', not 'ly' with a long i.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes careless or dismissive behavior that can seem arrogant or irresponsible.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cavalierly in formal writing, news, and serious criticism of how someone handled a responsibility. In casual talk, people more often say 'didn't care' or 'brushed it off'. It is usually used to criticize, not to describe harmless behavior.

distinctions.note: Carelessly means without attention to detail; cavalierly adds a sense of dismissive, almost arrogant indifference to consequences.
Casually describes a relaxed manner; cavalierly implies indifference to something that should matter.

examples.everyday: He shrugged cavalierly when I asked if he'd locked the car.
examples.professional: The manager cavalierly approved the budget without reading the forecast.
examples.analytical: Hegel cavalierly reduces centuries of religious practice to stages of Spirit, skipping the evidence that complicates his scheme.

nuance.analogy: Acting cavalierly is like tossing a valuable vase onto a shelf without looking, as if it were a paper cup.
nuance.etymology: From cavalier, from French cavalier 'horseman', plus the English adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the 'LEER' syllable.
Using cavalierly to mean kindly or politely; the meaning is careless or dismissive.

senses.definition: The act of cerebrating; reflection, thinking, thought.

core.definition: Thinking or reflection, especially deep or intellectual mental activity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BRAY, and say 'shun' for the ending. The first syllable has the 'air' vowel with a clear American r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly pompous. It can sound stuffy or intentionally lofty.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans rarely use this word in speech. You will find it in older books, essays, or formal writing, or in playful speech to sound lofty. In everyday talk, say thinking, reflection, or mental work.

distinctions.note: Reflection is common and conversational; cerebration sounds elevated and can be ironic.
Contemplation implies calm, sustained meditation, while cerebration is general intellectual work.

examples.everyday: After hours of cerebration, I finally figured out why the old recipe kept failing.
examples.professional: The planning session gave us time for real cerebration instead of just status updates.
examples.analytical: Descartes located cerebration in the thinking mind, sharply separating it from the body's passions.

nuance.analogy: Like a computer quietly running a long calculation in the background before it shows the result.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cerebrum (brain), through the verb cerebrate.
common_mistakes: Using cerebration in casual speech where thinking or reflection would be more natural.
Confusing cerebration with celebration because of the similar sound and spelling.

senses.definition: An item of furniture used to sit on or in, comprising a seat, legs or wheels, back, and sometimes arm rests, for use by one person.
senses.example: All I need to weather a snowstorm is hot coffee, a warm fire, a good book and a comfortable chair.

senses.definition: Clipping of chairperson.
senses.example: Under the rules of order adopted by the board, the chair may neither make nor second motions.

senses.definition: The post or position of chairperson.
senses.example: The meeting began, with Mr Roberts in the chair.

senses.definition: A cast-iron component used on railways to support bullhead rails and secure them to the sleepers.
Ellipsis of electric chair (“device used for performing execution”).
senses.example: The court will show no mercy; if he gets convicted, it's the chair for him.

senses.definition: A distinguished professorship at a university.
A vehicle for one person; either a sedan borne upon poles, or a two-wheeled carriage drawn by one horse; a gig.
The seat or office of a person in authority, such as a judge or bishop.
An assigned position in a beauty salon or barbershop.
senses.example: Melinda has the best chair in the salon.

senses.definition: The seating position of a particular musician in an orchestra.
senses.example: My violin teacher used to play first chair with the Boston Pops.

senses.definition: One of two possible conformers of cyclohexane rings (the other being boat), shaped roughly like a chair.
To act as chairperson at; to preside over.
senses.example: Bob will chair tomorrow's meeting.

senses.definition: To carry in a seated position upon one's shoulders, especially in celebration or victory.

core.definition: A seat for one person, usually with a back and legs, for sitting on. Also, the position of chairperson who leads a meeting.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable, and the vowel is the 'air' sound with an American 'r' coloring at the end, so do not say 'chay' or 'chur'. Learners often drop the 'r' or split the vowel into two sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. When used for a leader, 'chair' sounds professional and respectful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'chair' for furniture in homes, offices, and restaurants, and in meetings it refers to the person leading the discussion. As a verb, 'to chair a meeting' means to preside over it, and 'chairperson' or 'chair' is used for the leader. Asking 'Can I pull up a chair?' is a friendly, natural request in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Seat is a more general term that includes stools, benches, and car seats, while a chair is a piece of furniture with a back for one person.
A stool has no back or armrests, so it is not a chair in the usual American sense.
An armchair has arms and is usually more comfortable, while an ordinary chair may have no arms.

examples.everyday: Pull up a chair and tell me how the game went.
examples.professional: Maria will chair the Q3 planning review, so please send your slides to her by Monday.
examples.analytical: The chair of the committee controls the agenda, which quietly shapes what the group is able to discuss.

nuance.analogy: Like a conductor of an orchestra, a chair sets the tempo of a meeting and decides who speaks next.
nuance.etymology: From Old French chaiere, from Latin cathedra, from Greek kathedra 'seat'.
common_mistakes: Calling a sofa or couch a chair; a chair is for one person.
Pronouncing the word 'chur' or 'chay', which drops the American 'air' vowel.
Using 'chair' as a verb for sitting; the verb means to preside over a meeting or to carry someone in celebration.

chair.etymology: From Middle English *chayere*, *chayer*, *chayre*, from Old French *chaiere*, *chaere*, from Latin *cathedra* (“seat”), from Ancient Greek *καθέδρα*, from *κατά* (“down”) + *ἕδρα* (“seat”).

senses.definition: A malicious trickster; a fake person, especially one who deceives for personal profit.
senses.example: The television preacher was exposed as a charlatan who had been selling fake miracle cures.

core.definition: A person who falsely claims special skill or knowledge and deceives others, usually to gain money, status, or influence.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the initial ch is pronounced sh, as in French. The final syllable is reduced to a weak 'tuhn', so do not add a full vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative: it calls someone a fraud. Use it carefully about real people, since it accuses them of deliberate deception.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use charlatan for fake experts, such as a wellness guru selling miracle cures or a consultant with false credentials. It is fairly formal and appears often in news and commentary. In casual talk, people more often say fraud, con artist, or phony.

distinctions.note: A fraud is anything or anyone that is fake or deceptive; charlatan emphasizes a person who poses as an expert.
A quack claims medical skill falsely; charlatan is broader and covers any field where someone pretends to know more.
An impostor pretends to be a specific other person; a charlatan pretends to have skills or knowledge that they lack.

collocations: a charlatan posing as an expert

examples.everyday: My uncle sold us a miracle cure for his back pain, and it turned out he was a total charlatan.
examples.professional: The vendor promised machine learning results without any clean data, and after the pilot we realized he was a charlatan.
examples.analytical: Critics have long described some of the Sophists as charlatans who sold the appearance of wisdom without rigorous knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like a stage magician who claims real powers and sells the trick as truth.
nuance.etymology: From Italian ciarlatano, a babbler or quack, from ciarlare, to chatter.
common_mistakes: Using charlatan for an honest mistake; the word implies deliberate deception.
Pronouncing the ch as in cheese; it is an sh sound, like the start of shar-luh-tuhn.

charlatan.etymology: From Middle French *charlatan*, from *ciarlatano* (“quack”), a blend of *ciarlatore* (“chatterer”) + *cerretano* (“hawker, quack”).

senses.definition: Any object used as a wedge or filler, especially when placed behind a wheel to prevent it from rolling.
senses.example: He kicked a chock under the trailer's tire so it would not roll down the driveway.

senses.definition: Any fitting or fixture used to restrict movement, especially movement of a line; traditionally was a fixture near a bulwark with two horns pointing towards each other, with a gap between where the line can be inserted.
senses.example: The deckhand ran the mooring line through the chock before cleating it on the dock.

senses.definition: (historical) An illicit, fermented alcoholic beverage brewed on-site.
senses.example: In the hills, families once brewed chock in backyard stills during Prohibition.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To stop or fasten, as with a wedge, or block; to scotch.
senses.example: The driver chocked the wheels with bricks before climbing under the truck.

senses.definition: To make a dull sound.
senses.example: The old wooden gate chocked softly as the wind pushed it closed.

senses.definition: To insert a line in a chock.
senses.example: The sailor chocked the line through the fairlead before tightening the halyard.

senses.definition: Representing a dull sound.
senses.example: Chock went the wooden mallet against the stubborn log, splitting it cleanly.

senses.definition: Entirely; quite.
senses.example: The fridge was chock-full of leftovers from the holiday weekend.

core.definition: A block or wedge placed against a wheel or object to keep it from rolling or moving.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with the open 'ah' vowel of 'hot' (the cot-caught merger), not the 'aw' of 'chalk'. Say the 'ch' as in 'church' and do not add a vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It is a safety word on job sites, roads and boats, so it signals care rather than danger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'wheel chock' or 'chock' for the block placed under a tire, especially on trucks, trailers, aircraft and construction equipment. 'To chock the wheels' is standard safety language. A boat chock is a separate sense: a metal fitting on a deck or rail that guides a line. Most people who are unsure say 'wheel chock' or 'wedge'.

distinctions.note: A wedge is any tapered piece of material; a chock is a purpose-made block used to stop movement, especially of wheels.
A brake slows or stops a wheel through friction in its system; a chock physically blocks the wheel and is used when a vehicle is parked or left unattended.

examples.everyday: Put a chock behind the back tire before you crawl under the car.
examples.professional: The crew chocked the wheels before they started unloading the trailer.
examples.analytical: A chock restricts movement without fixing the load, so it is only a partial safeguard against rolling.

nuance.analogy: A chock works like a doorstop for a wheel.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'chalk' (/tʃɔk/); General American uses the open 'ah' vowel of 'hot'.
Saying 'chock the car' without naming the wheels or tires, which is the usual American safety phrasing.

chock.etymology: From Middle English **chokke*, from Anglo-Norman *choque* (compare modern Norman *chouque*), from an variant of Old French *çouche*, *çouche* (“block, log”), of origin, from **tsukka* (compare, Old Irish *tócht* (“part, piece”), itself a metathetic…

senses.definition: To design and record the choreography for a dramatic work such as a ballet.
senses.example: She choreographed the second act of the ballet over three long months in the studio.

senses.definition: To direct the development of a project; to orchestrate.
senses.example: The senator choreographed the rollout so every committee announced its plan on the same day.

senses.definition: To work as a choreographer.
senses.example: After college, he choreographed for a small dance company in Chicago and two regional theaters.

core.definition: To design and arrange the steps and movements of a dance or ballet, or to plan and coordinate the stages of a complex event.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ee-uh- is quick and reduced, not a separate long 'eye' sound, and the final syllable rhymes with 'staff'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests skillful planning, especially of movement or events.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use choreograph for dance, theater, film, and music performances, and sometimes in business for carefully planned events such as a product launch. It is less common for everyday tasks, and in those cases people usually say plan or organize. The verb is often used in the passive, as in 'The show was choreographed by a former dancer.'

distinctions.note: Direct is a general word for leading a show or project; choreograph refers specifically to designing the movements or planned sequence of action.
Stage means to arrange a performance or event, often including scenery and action, while choreograph focuses on the planned movements.

examples.everyday: My sister choreographed a dance routine for her friends' wedding.
examples.professional: We choreographed the product launch so the demos, speeches, and video all happen in the right order.
examples.analytical: Foucault's account of institutions shows how social spaces are choreographed to shape the bodies that move through them.

nuance.analogy: Like a conductor setting the tempo for every section of an orchestra, choreographing arranges each movement in its proper place.
nuance.etymology: From Greek khoreia, dance, and graphein, to write.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as CHOR-ee-oh-graph with a long o; the American form is KOR-ee-uh-graf.
Using choreograph for any kind of planning; it usually implies careful arrangement of movement or action.

senses.definition: A group of singers and dancers in a theatrical performance or religious festival who commented on the main performance in speech or song.
senses.example: In the Greek play, the chorus of singers and dancers commented on the hero's downfall.

senses.definition: A song performed by the singers of such a group.
senses.example: The audience applauded when the chorus sang its rousing final song.

senses.definition: A group of singers performing together; a choir; specifically, such a group singing together in a musical, an opera, etc. as distinct from the soloists; an ensemble.
senses.example: The performance of the chorus was awe-inspiring and exhilarating.

senses.definition: A group of people in a performance who recite together.
senses.example: In the classroom play, the chorus recited the poem line by line together.

senses.definition: An instance of singing by a group of people.
senses.example: Everyone joined in a loud chorus of Happy Birthday at the party.

senses.definition: A group of angels, or of types of angels like seraphim.
senses.example: Medieval paintings often show a chorus of angels singing around the throne of God.

senses.definition: A group of people, animals, or inanimate objects who make sounds together.
senses.example: a chorus of crickets a chorus of whiners

senses.definition: The noise or sound made by such a group.
senses.example: a chorus of shouts and catcalls

senses.definition: A group of people who express a unanimous opinion.
senses.example: Reporters formed a chorus that demanded the senator resign immediately.

senses.definition: The opinion expressed by such a group.
senses.example: The senator ignored the chorus of criticism coming from her own party.

senses.definition: A piece of music, especially one in a larger work such as an opera, written to be sung by a choir in parts (for example, by sopranos, altos, tenors, and basses).
senses.example: The chorus of Verdi's opera rises dramatically in the third act.

senses.definition: A part of a song which is repeated between verses to emphasize the song's content; a refrain.
senses.example: The catchiest part of most songs is the chorus.

senses.definition: The main part of a pop song played after the introduction.
A group of organ pipes or organ stops intended to be played simultaneously; a compound stop; also, the sound made by such pipes or stops.
senses.example: The organist engaged a bright chorus of pipes to add brilliance to the hymn.

senses.definition: A feature or setting in electronic music that makes one instrument sound like many.
senses.example: The synthesizer's chorus effect made a single voice sound like a whole ensemble.

senses.definition: A simple, often repetitive, song intended to be sung in a group during informal worship.
senses.example: The youth group closed the service by singing a simple chorus everyone knew by heart.

senses.definition: The improvised solo section in a small group performance.
senses.example: The saxophonist took a blistering chorus after the pianist finished his solo.

senses.definition: To sing (a song), express (a sentiment), or recite or say (words) in chorus.
senses.example: The fans chorused the team's anthem as the players walked onto the field.

senses.definition: To express concurrence with (something said by another person); to echo.
senses.example: Every colleague chorused the director's remark that the deadline was unrealistic.

senses.definition: To sing the chorus or refrain of a song.
senses.example: Everyone in the pew chorused the refrain on the final verse of the hymn.

senses.definition: To sing, express, or say in, or as if in, unison.
senses.example: The students chorused the answer in unison, and the teacher smiled.

senses.definition: To echo in unison another person's words.
Of animals: to make cries or sounds together.
(rare) To provide (a song) with a chorus or refrain.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The part of a song that repeats after each verse, usually with the main melody and the title words.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ch' is a hard k sound, not the 'ch' of church. The second syllable is weak, like 'us' with a reduced vowel, so don't add an extra 'ka' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; calling a song's chorus catchy is praise, but the word itself carries no strong feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the chorus' for the repeated refrain of a song, as in 'What's the chorus?' or 'I can't remember the chorus.' For a group of singers in a church or school, they more often say 'choir', though 'chorus' is used for a community or school singing group. The phrase 'in chorus' is common in speech, meaning 'all together, out loud.'

distinctions.note: A choir is an organized group of singers, usually in a church or school; chorus is the more general term, and in musicals and operas it means the group that is not the soloists.
A verse tells part of the story and changes each time, while the chorus repeats the same words and melody.

examples.everyday: Come on, sing the chorus with me, it's the only part I actually know.
examples.professional: The launch dashboard was a chorus of complaints about latency, so we moved the fix to the top of the sprint.
examples.analytical: In classical drama, the Greek chorus comments on the action and voices the community's moral judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a familiar refrain you hear again and again on the radio, pulling you back to the main idea.
nuance.etymology: From Latin chorus, from Greek choros, a dance performed by a group, often with song.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'ch' like the 'ch' in church; it is a k sound.
Using chorus to mean a church choir in everyday American speech; 'choir' is the usual word.

chorus.etymology: The noun is borrowed from Medieval Latin *chorus* (“church choir”), Latin *chorus* (“group of dancers and singers; dance”), from Ancient Greek *χορός* (“group of dancers and singers, choir, chorus; dance accompanied by song; round dance”); The verb is…

senses.definition: In a chronological manner; with reference to time.
senses.example: He had aged but a year chronologically, but in appearance a decade.

senses.definition: In sequence according to time.
senses.example: His chapters are arranged thematically, not chronologically.

core.definition: In the order in which events happened in time, from earliest to latest.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'LAH' in the middle, with a lighter stress on 'krah' at the start. The 'o' in 'chrono' is a short vowel, and the ending '-ly' is pronounced 'klee', not 'lee' alone.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes arrangement and carries no judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chronologically in writing, presentations, and conversation when they want to say that things are arranged by date or time. In casual speech people often say 'in order' or 'in the order they happened', which is more natural in everyday talk. Chronologically is a good choice for reports, history, and project timelines.

distinctions.note: Sequentially means in a set order, which may be numerical or logical, while chronologically specifically means by time.
In order is broader and casual, while chronologically is precise and suggests a timeline.

examples.everyday: Can you tell me the story of your trip chronologically, starting from the day you left?
examples.professional: Please sort the incident reports chronologically so we can see when the outage started.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the documents should be read chronologically to show how the policy changed over time.

nuance.analogy: Chronologically is like a row of dominoes falling in the exact order they were set up, from first to last.
nuance.etymology: From chronological, from Greek chronos (time) and logos (word, reason).
common_mistakes: Using chronologically for things that are merely in a list, where 'in order' or 'sequentially' fits better.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'kro-no-LOJ-ik-lee' with the wrong vowel.

senses.definition: A Christian house of worship; a building where Christian religious services take place.
senses.example: There is a lovely little church in the valley.

senses.definition: Christians collectively seen as a single spiritual community; Christianity; Christendom.
senses.example: These worshippers make up the Church of Christ.

senses.definition: A local group of people who follow the same Christian religious beliefs, local or general.
senses.example: Our church holds a potluck dinner every second Sunday, and everyone is welcome.

senses.definition: A particular denomination of Christianity.
senses.example: The Church of England separated from the Roman Catholic Church in 1534.

senses.definition: Christian worship held at a church; service.
senses.example: We go to church at ten o'clock, then have coffee in the fellowship hall.

senses.definition: Organized religion in general or a specific religion considered as a political institution.
senses.example: Many constitutions enshrine the separation of church and state.

senses.definition: Any religious group or place of worship; a temple.
senses.example: She goes to a Wiccan church down the road.

senses.definition: (historical) To conduct a religious service for (a woman after childbirth, or a newly married couple).
senses.example: After she gave birth, the village priest churched her in a short ceremony.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To educate someone religiously, as in a church.
senses.example: The mission school sought to church the children in the faith and its customs.

senses.definition: Used to express strong agreement.
senses.example: – These burritos are the best! – Church!

core.definition: A building for Christian worship, or the community of Christians, whether a local congregation or all believers together.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with an r-colored vowel (like 'her') between two 'ch' sounds. Do not add a vowel before or after, and do not drop the r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; positive or negative depending on a person's view of religion. Capital 'Church' can signal the universal body of believers or a specific institution.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'go to church' without 'the' for attending services. 'The church' may mean a building or an institution, such as the Catholic Church. It also names a congregation: 'Our church is growing.' 'Church' as an interjection of agreement is slang from African American Christian culture.

distinctions.note: A chapel is a smaller place of worship, often within a school, hospital, or larger church.
A congregation is the group of people who worship together, not the building.
A denomination is a larger organized family of churches, such as Baptist or Lutheran.

examples.everyday: We usually go to church on Sunday morning and then grab brunch.
examples.professional: The church hosts a food pantry and partners with local nonprofits.
examples.analytical: The Reformers debated whether the true church is defined by right preaching of the Word and right administration of the sacraments.

nuance.analogy: The church is a family gathering that is also a building, a worship service, and a worldwide people.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cirice, from Greek kyriakon, 'the Lord's house.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'go to the church' for attending services; say 'go to church.'
Pronouncing it with two syllables or dropping the r sound.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is ekklesia, 'assembly' or 'called-out gathering.' Matthew 16:18 records Jesus saying he will build his church. Acts 2:42-47 describes the early church's teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer. Ephesians 1:22-23 presents the church as Christ's body, with Christ as head.

traditions.view: The Church is the one, holy, catholic, and apostolic body, a communion centered on the Eucharist and the bishop, and the Orthodox Church understands itself as that Church.
The Church is the one visible society founded by Christ, governed by the pope and bishops, and the means of grace through the sacraments.

Protestants often distinguish the visible church of local congregations from the invisible church of all true believers. Lutherans and Reformed stress word and sacrament; Baptists stress a gathered community of believers.

church.etymology: From Middle English *chirche*, from Old English *ċiriċe* (“church”), from **kirikā*, an early borrowing of Ancient Greek *κυριακόν*, neuter form of *κυριακός* (“belonging to the lord”), from *κύριος* (“ruler, lord”), from Proto-Indo-European **ḱewh₁-* (“to…

senses.definition: In a civil manner; politely.
senses.example: The two candidates spoke civilly during the debate, despite their sharp disagreements.

core.definition: In a polite and respectful way, even when people disagree or are in conflict.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle 'l' often works as a syllable on its own, so the word sounds like 'SIV-l-ee' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests restraint and good manners, especially when the situation could have turned hostile.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'civilly' often in phrases like 'talk civilly', 'disagree civilly', or 'ask civilly'. It is a little more formal than 'politely', and it often implies that the speakers could have been rude but chose not to be. In casual speech, 'nicely' or 'politely' is more common.

distinctions.note: Politely is the general word for good manners, while civilly often implies restraint in a tense or disagreeable situation.
Courteously is more formal and literary, while civilly is common in American everyday and professional speech.

examples.everyday: Even though we argued about the bill, we talked civilly the whole time.
examples.professional: In the meeting, the two teams disagreed civilly and agreed to revisit the design next week.
examples.analytical: The two philosophers debated civilly, though their underlying positions could not have been more opposed.

nuance.analogy: Speaking civilly is like keeping your hands on the wheel during a heated argument: you can still drive, even when the road is rough.
nuance.etymology: From civil, from Latin civilis, relating to citizens, plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'civilly' to mean 'civilized' in general, such as 'a civilly society'; the adjective is 'civil' or 'civilized'.
Confusing it with 'civically', which means in a way relating to citizenship or community life.

senses.definition: A differential form whose exterior derivative is zero.
senses.example: Every exact form is also a closed form, since its exterior derivative vanishes.

senses.definition: A form (expression) that does not use limits, implicitly or explicitly.
senses.example: There is no known representation of π in closed form: each expression for it includes an integral, an infinite series, or an infinite continued fraction.

senses.definition: A type of poetry with regular structure, such as meter or a rhyming pattern.
senses.example: The sonnet is a closed form, so its fourteen lines follow a strict rhyme scheme.

senses.definition: Trobar clus.
senses.example: Her seminar examined how the troubadours used closed form to hide meaning from outsiders.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see closed,‎ form.
senses.example: If ω is a closed form, then dω=0.

core.definition: A mathematical expression that computes a result directly with a finite number of standard operations, without limits or infinite sums.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FORM, and the vowel is the or sound with a clear American r after it, not a long oo. Closed is stressed less and ends with a plain d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians, statisticians, physicists, and data scientists use closed form in lectures, papers, and problem sets. Americans say 'find a closed form' or 'there's no closed form' in conversation among experts. Outside technical settings, people would say 'an exact formula' instead.

distinctions.note: A closed form gives an exact answer as a formula, while a numerical solution gets an approximate answer by computation.
An infinite series is a sum of infinitely many terms, and a closed form rewrites that sum as a finite expression.

examples.everyday: My kid asked how to find the area of a circle, and I told him the closed form is pi times r squared.
examples.professional: The optimizer doesn't have a closed form, so we estimate the parameters with gradient descent.
examples.analytical: A closed form expresses the sum directly in terms of n, so it gives the value for any n without adding every term.

nuance.analogy: A closed form is like a shortcut formula on a map: it takes you to the destination without making you walk every street.
nuance.etymology: Closed from Middle English closed, and form from Latin forma meaning shape.
common_mistakes: Writing 'close form' instead of closed form, since the adjective needs the -d.
Assuming every equation has a closed form; many problems have none, and numerical methods are used instead.

senses.definition: To fill up or choke up; to stop up.
senses.example: Silt from the storm began to cloy the drainage pipes until water backed up across the yard.

senses.definition: To clog, to glut, or satisfy, as the appetite; to satiate.
senses.example: Heavy meals at the buffet seemed to cloy my appetite before I reached the dessert table.

senses.definition: To fill to loathing; to surfeit.
senses.example: Too many sweet, sugary songs on the radio can cloy listeners until they switch channels.

core.definition: To become unpleasant or tiresome through excess, especially of something sweet or overly sentimental.

pronunciation.tip: Cloy rhymes with boy and toy, using the oy diphthong. Don't pronounce it with a long o sound like 'kloh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that too much of something good becomes unpleasant.
nuance.usage_note: Cloy is mostly used in writing, reviews, and literary criticism. In speech Americans usually say 'it gets too sweet' or 'too much after a while.' Use cloy when you want to sound precise about excess that turns unpleasant.

distinctions.note: Satiate means fully satisfy an appetite, while cloy means excess makes the pleasure unpleasant.
