pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, spee. Many learners say the middle syllables too clearly; in American speech the -ience ending is reduced to a short "uns".

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expedience in writing and formal discussion, often about decisions made for practical reasons. It is rarely used in casual talk, where people say "the quick way" or "what's easiest." It can sound judgmental when it implies that practical concerns outweigh principle.

distinctions.note: Expedience usually means the quality of being useful for a purpose; expediency more often implies choosing a course of action for practical gain, sometimes at the cost of principle.
Convenience is ordinary comfort or ease, while expedience carries a sense of purpose and urgency about achieving a result.

examples.everyday: We ordered pizza for the party, mostly out of expedience, since nobody had time to cook.
examples.professional: We chose the cheaper vendor out of expedience, since they could deliver the servers before the deadline.
examples.analytical: Some policies are adopted for expedience rather than for principle, and this makes their justification depend heavily on context.

nuance.analogy: Expedience is the shortcut across the field: it gets you there faster, but it is not always the path you would choose if you had time.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expedire, "to free the feet, extricate," from ex- and pes, pedis, "foot."
common_mistakes: Using expedience as a synonym for speed; it refers to suitability for a purpose, not only to hurry.
Stressing the last syllable, as in ex-pe-di-ENCE.

expedience.etymology: From Middle English *expedience*, from Old French *expedience*, from Late Latin *expedientia*, from Latin *expediens*.

senses.definition: The process of calculating a power by multiplying together a number of equal factors, where the exponent specifies the number of factors to multiply.
senses.example: In 5 the base is 5 and the power is 4, so there are 4 identical factors of 5, and exponentiation gives 625 as the result.

senses.definition: A mathematical problem involving exponentiation.
senses.example: The final exam included a tricky problem involving exponentiation with negative fractional exponents.

core.definition: The operation of raising a number to a power, meaning multiplying a base by itself as many times as the exponent says.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AY, the fourth syllable, and the -shun ending is a reduced schwa sound. Learners often stress the -nen syllable instead, so keep the stress late in the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it carries no emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exponentiation in math classes, programming and data science, usually when talking about raising numbers to powers. In everyday talk it is rare and would sound overly technical, so people often say 'raising to a power' instead. A natural reply in a technical discussion is a short confirmation or a follow-up question about the base or exponent.

distinctions.note: Multiplication repeats addition, while exponentiation repeats multiplication of the same base.
Power can mean the result or the exponent itself, while exponentiation names the operation.

examples.everyday: My kid asked why two to the tenth power is so big, and I explained that it's just a form of exponentiation.
examples.professional: The encryption library uses modular exponentiation, so the runtime stays reasonable even with large keys.
examples.analytical: Exponentiation is not commutative, since a to the power b generally differs from b to the power a, which constrains the algebraic laws we can assume.

nuance.analogy: Exponentiation is repeated multiplication just as multiplication is repeated addition.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exponere, to set forth, via exponent and the suffix -ation.
common_mistakes: Confusing exponentiation with multiplication, for example treating 2 to the 3rd as 2 times 3.
Pronouncing the middle syllables with full vowels instead of reduced ones.

senses.definition: A person who expounds or explains.

core.definition: A person who explains or interprets a subject, text or doctrine in detail.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -SPOWND-, and the vowel is the diphthong /aʊ/ as in 'out', not the 'oh' of 'expose'. The final -er is a reduced /ɚ/ sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it implies someone who clarifies a complex subject, sometimes with authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expounder mainly in religious, academic or literary writing about someone who explains a doctrine, law or theory in depth. In everyday speech, they say 'explainer', 'advocate' or 'teacher'. The word is less common than expositor, so use expositor if you want the more standard term.

distinctions.note: Both mean someone who explains; expositor is more common in formal and academic writing, while expounder is less frequent and sounds more personal or rhetorical.
An advocate argues for a position, while an expounder explains it in detail, though they may also favor it.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is an expounder of the tax rules, so I always ask him before I file.
examples.professional: As the team's expounder of the new metrics, she walked everyone through each assumption in the quarterly review.
examples.analytical: Kant is a rigorous expounder of moral duty, insisting that reason alone must ground the categorical imperative.

nuance.analogy: Like a guide who explains each stop on a long tour, rather than just pointing out the sights.
nuance.etymology: From expound, from Latin exponere, 'to set out'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'EX-pound' or using the 'oh' vowel of 'expose'; the stress is on the second syllable with the 'ow' of 'out'.
Using expounder for a casual speaker; the word implies detailed, careful explanation.

senses.definition: In a facetious or flippant manner; in a manner that treats serious issues with deliberately inappropriate humor.
senses.example: When asked about the layoffs, he facetiously suggested we all take up competitive napping.

senses.definition: (dated) In a pleasantly humorous or playful fashion.
senses.example: The old letter began facetiously, addressing her as the queen of all the dance halls.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: In a joking or flippant way that treats a serious matter lightly or inappropriately.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SEE. The final -ly is a light 'lee,' and the middle 'shus' is weak and quick.

nuance.connotation: Negative or disapproving; it describes a joke or remark that seems out of place.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use facetiously in writing or formal speech to describe how someone said something, such as 'He answered facetiously.' In casual speech, people more often say 'he was just joking' or 'he was being sarcastic.' It signals that the speaker did not intend the remark seriously.

distinctions.note: Sarcastically implies mocking or saying the opposite of what is meant, while facetiously stresses inappropriate joking.
Jokingly is neutral and friendly, but facetiously often carries mild criticism.

examples.everyday: When I asked if the pizza was ready, he said facetiously, 'Sure, it's been ready since Tuesday.'
examples.professional: She replied facetiously to the deadline question, which made the meeting tense for a minute.
examples.analytical: The author writes facetiously about religious ritual, but the joke exposes a real tension in the argument.

nuance.analogy: Speaking facetiously is like wearing a party hat to a board meeting: the spirit is playful, but the setting is wrong.
nuance.etymology: Formed from facetious with the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllables as separate strong syllables; the 'shus' part is weak.
Using facetiously to mean seriously or politely.

senses.definition: To create a list of the factors of.
senses.example: Before computing the greatest common divisor, she factorized each number to list all its factors.

senses.definition: To divide an expression into a list of items that, when multiplied together, will produce the original quantity.
senses.example: To solve the equation, he factorized x squared minus nine into x minus three times x plus three.

senses.definition: To warn not to pay or give up goods.
senses.example: The creditor's lawyer factorized the employer, warning it not to pay the debtor's wages directly.

senses.definition: To attach the effects of a debtor in the hands of a third party.
senses.example: The court factorized the debtor's wages held by his employer until the outstanding loan was repaid.

core.definition: To break a number or algebraic expression into factors that multiply together to give the original quantity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAK, with a lighter secondary stress on the rize syllable, which rhymes with eyes. The middle syllable is a quick, reduced uh, so do not say fak-TOR-ize.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical verb.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use factorize mostly in math and computer science, while factor is the more everyday verb, as in 'factor this polynomial'. Factorize is slightly more formal and appears often in textbooks and programming. The obsolete legal sense of warning someone not to pay is not used in American English.

distinctions.note: Factor is the more common everyday verb in American math and speech, while factorize is a bit more formal and frequent in computing.
Expand multiplies a product out into a sum, while factorize goes the other way, breaking a sum into a product.

examples.everyday: My nephew asked how to factorize 30 for his homework, and I told him it's 2 times 3 times 5.
examples.professional: The test suite factorizes the sample numbers into primes to check that the encryption code behaves correctly.
examples.analytical: Factorizing a large polynomial over the integers can be far harder than checking that a proposed factorization is correct.

nuance.analogy: Like unmixing a smoothie back into the fruit that went into it.
nuance.etymology: From factor plus the English suffix -ize, from Greek -izein, meaning to make into or to treat in a certain way.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling factorise in American writing; the American spelling is factorize.
Using factorize in everyday speech to mean any splitting into parts; ordinary speakers say break down or split up.

senses.definition: The loss of one's social position, prestige, status, power, etc.
senses.example: After the scandal, the senator's fall from grace was swift and public.

senses.definition: To lose God's favor through sins or wrongdoings.
senses.example: The priest feared he would fall from grace if he kept hiding his sins.

senses.definition: To fall from one's current social position to something lower, to lose one's prestige, status or power.
senses.example: His father fell from grace with the emperor.

core.definition: A loss of status, reputation or favor, often after a scandal or failure; in theology, losing God's favor through sin.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'grace'. 'From' reduces to 'frum', and the r in 'from' and 'grace' should be clear. 'Fall' sounds like 'fawl' (cot-caught merger: 'fahl' for many).

nuance.connotation: Negative: disgrace, disappointment, loss of respect. In theology it can be serious or neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly use it in news and conversation about public figures who lose respect after a scandal. It is used as 'a fall from grace' or 'fall from grace' (verb phrase: 'fell from grace'). In religion it refers to losing God's favor.

distinctions.note: Downfall refers to a ruin or cause of ruin; fall from grace emphasizes losing favor or esteem.
Disgrace is the shame itself, while fall from grace is the process of losing standing.
Apostasy is deliberately abandoning one's faith, which is narrower than falling from grace.

examples.everyday: Did you hear about the senator's fall from grace after that scandal?
examples.professional: The company's fall from grace followed the accounting investigation.
examples.analytical: Tragic narratives often track a protagonist's fall from grace, driven by pride or a fatal flaw.

nuance.analogy: It is like a star that once stood high in the sky and sinks below the horizon.
nuance.etymology: From 'grace' in the sense of favor, with the theological sense of falling from God's favor through sin; from Latin gratia 'favor'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'fall of grace' or 'fall to grace'.
Using it for a simple mistake that has no real loss of status.
Pronouncing 'grace' as 'gras'.
nuance.biblical_note: The idea is in the RSV of Galatians 5:4, which warns those seeking justification by the law that they have fallen away from grace. The Greek is exepesate, 'you have fallen out of'. Hebrews 12:15 urges believers to see that no one fails to obtain the grace of God. Genesis 3 describes the fall of Adam and Eve from their original state, though without using this phrase.

traditions.view: Emphasizes that humans can turn away from God's life and grace through sin and are restored through repentance and the sacraments; grace is God's uncreated energy and the Fall of Adam is understood as ancestral sin and mortality rather than inherited guilt.
Teaches that mortal sin destroys sanctifying grace in the soul, and that it can be restored through repentance and the sacrament of Penance.

Views differ: Lutherans and Arminians (including Methodists and many Pentecostals) allow that a believer can fall away from grace, while Reformed (Calvinist) Christians teach the perseverance of the saints, so that true believers do not finally lose grace. Many Baptists affirm eternal security.

senses.definition: Wonderful; marvelous; excellent; extraordinarily good or great (used especially as an intensifier).
senses.example: "I had a simply fantastic vacation, and I can't wait to tell you all about it!"

senses.definition: Existing in or constructed from fantasy; of or relating to fantasy; fanciful.
senses.example: He told fantastic stories of dragons and goblins.

senses.definition: (rare) Given to fanciful ideas, impulsive; irrational.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Extremely good or wonderful; used to express enthusiasm or strong approval about something you like.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the second syllable, TAS. The first vowel is the short a of fan, not the air sound of fair, and the final k is often lightly released.

nuance.connotation: Strongly positive. It is enthusiastic and friendly, though very common, so it can sound casual or overused in formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say fantastic often as a warm reply, like That's fantastic, or That sounds fantastic, in casual conversation. In professional settings, it is fine for praise, but great or excellent may sound more measured. Americans also use fantastic to describe food, weather, or an experience.

distinctions.note: Fantastical means strange or imaginary, often in a literary way, while fantastic in everyday speech means wonderful.
Fabulous is also enthusiastic but feels a bit more stylish or glamorous, while fantastic is broader and more neutral.

examples.everyday: Your pasta is fantastic, honestly; what did you put in the sauce?
examples.professional: The Q3 numbers are fantastic, so great work, team.
examples.analytical: Although the proof is fantastic in its elegance, it depends on a lemma we have not yet verified.

nuance.analogy: Like a firework: bright, loud, and meant to make you cheer.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin fantasticus, from Greek phantastikos, meaning able to imagine.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as FAN-tastic, instead of fan-TAS-tik.
Using fantastic in formal writing where excellent or remarkable would fit better.

fantastic.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *fantastique*, borrowed from Late Latin *phantasticus*, borrowed from Ancient Greek *φᾰντᾰστῐκός* (“imaginary, fantastic; fictional”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **bʰeh₂-* (“to shine”).

senses.definition: A wish of happiness or safety at parting, especially a permanent departure.
senses.example: He bid farewell to all of his fans.

senses.definition: A departure; the act of leaving.
senses.example: The farewell at the airport was quick, but her hug lasted a long time.

senses.definition: Parting, valedictory, final.
senses.example: a farewell discourse; the band's farewell tour

senses.definition: Goodbye.
senses.example: He said "Farewell!" and left.

senses.definition: To bid farewell or say goodbye.
senses.example: She farewelled the team with a short speech and a box of donuts.

core.definition: A goodbye, especially a parting that may be long or permanent, or the act of saying goodbye.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'well.' Keep the r in 'fair' pronounced, and make the first vowel an open e sound, as in 'bed.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to emotional. It suggests a significant or sometimes sad departure, so it can sound dramatic in casual situations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'farewell' most often as a noun in phrases like 'farewell party,' 'farewell tour' or 'farewell speech.' As a casual goodbye at the end of a phone call or workday, 'bye' or 'see you' is much more natural. The interjection 'farewell' sounds old-fashioned, literary or theatrical in modern American English.

distinctions.note: 'Goodbye' is the everyday word for parting; 'farewell' is more formal, emotional or ceremonial, and often implies a longer or final separation.
'Departure' is about the act of leaving; 'farewell' focuses on the good wishes and the emotional moment of parting.

examples.everyday: We had a small farewell dinner for Maria before she moved to Denver.
examples.professional: The team held a farewell lunch for our former lead engineer, who is moving to a new role at another company.
examples.analytical: The letter ends with a formal farewell that reads as both a blessing and a final acknowledgment of the long friendship.

nuance.analogy: A farewell is like the final bow at the end of a long performance: it marks the ending and sends the audience off with good wishes.
nuance.etymology: From 'fare,' meaning to go or travel, plus 'well,' so the phrase means 'go well' or 'fare well.'
common_mistakes: Using 'farewell' as a casual everyday goodbye, which can sound overly dramatic; 'bye' or 'see you later' is more natural.
Saying 'say farewell' when 'say goodbye' or 'bid farewell' is more natural in ordinary American English.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Revised Standard Version, 'farewell' appears in Second Corinthians 13:11 and Acts 15:29, where it translates the Greek word 'chairete,' which means 'rejoice' or 'be glad' and was used as a common greeting or closing in letters. Second Corinthians 13:11 closes Paul's letter with a call to mend ways, live in peace and rejoice. Acts 15:29 ends the letter sent from the Jerusalem council to the Gentile believers with a closing greeting.

farewell.etymology: From Middle English *farewel*, from *fare wel!*, an imperative expression, possibly further derived from Old English **far wel!*, equivalent to *fare* + *well*, said to somebody setting out on a journey.

senses.definition: A place where agricultural and similar activities take place, especially the growing of crops or the raising of livestock.
A tract of land held on lease for the purpose of cultivation.
A location used for an industrial purpose, having many similar structures.
senses.example: antenna farm; fuel farm; solar farm; wind farm

senses.definition: A group of coordinated servers.
senses.example: a render farm

senses.definition: The body of farmers of public revenues.
The condition of being let at a fixed rent; lease; a lease.

(historical) A fixed yearly sum accepted from a person as a composition for taxes or other moneys which he is empowered to collect; also, a fixed charge imposed on a town, county, etc. in respect of a tax or taxes to be collected within its limits.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) The letting-out of public revenue to a ‘farmer’; the privilege of farming a tax or taxes.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A baby farm.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To work on a farm, especially in the growing and harvesting of crops.
To devote (land) to farming.
To grow (a particular crop).
To give up to another, as an estate, a business, the revenue, etc. on condition of receiving in return a percentage of what it yields; to farm out.
senses.example: to farm the taxes

senses.definition: To engage in grinding (repetitive activity) in a particular area or against specific enemies for a particular drop or item.
To cultivate and/or disseminate through artificial algorithm-incentivized means.
To act performatively or deliberately to elicit a desired response.

core.definition: An area of land and buildings where crops are grown or animals are raised for food or products.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce the r clearly and make the vowel open, as in 'father,' with the r after it. Do not turn the word into 'fam,' which is a common error for speakers who drop the r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Farms are often associated with hard work, rural life and healthy food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'farm' in everyday speech for everything from a family homestead to a large corporate operation. Phrases like 'dairy farm,' 'farm stand' and 'farm-to-table' are common in restaurants and grocery stores. When you mean a very large industrial operation, Americans often say 'agribusiness' or 'feedlot' in technical contexts.

distinctions.note: A 'ranch' is usually a large area for raising livestock, especially cattle or horses, in the western United States, while a 'farm' often focuses on crops.
A 'plantation' is a large estate, historically associated with cash crops and forced labor, and the term carries serious historical connotations.

examples.everyday: We drove out to a farm near the lake to pick apples this weekend.
examples.professional: Our supply chain team now sources produce directly from a few regional farms to reduce transport delays.
examples.analytical: The moral significance of the farm as a place of labor and rest recurs in many agrarian writers of the nineteenth century.

nuance.analogy: A farm is like a kitchen on a large scale: planning, timing and care determine whether the harvest feeds the table.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English ferme, from Old French ferme meaning a fixed payment or lease, from Medieval Latin firma, a fixed rent.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing 'farm' as 'fam' by dropping the r sound.
Using 'farm' for a ranch with only cattle; Americans often say 'ranch' for large livestock operations in the West.

farm.etymology: Middle English *ferme*, *farme* (“rent, revenue, produce, factor, stewardship, meal, feast”), influenced by Anglo-Norman *ferme* (“rent, lease, farm”), from Medieval Latin *ferma*, *firma*.

senses.definition: The characteristic, state or condition of being female.

core.definition: The quality or condition of being female, especially in a biological sense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FEE; the ending -ness is a short 'nis,' with the vowel of 'bit.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is precise and clinical, and it is rarely used in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use femaleness. It appears mostly in academic or scientific writing about biology or in discussions of gender. In everyday talk, say being a woman or simply female when describing biology.

distinctions.note: Femaleness refers to biological sex; femininity refers to socially associated traits and style.
Womanhood is the everyday word for being an adult woman, including identity and experience.

examples.everyday: I don't think femaleness should decide what job someone gets, since it has nothing to do with the work.
examples.professional: The study controlled for femaleness at birth, not for gender identity, so its findings have a narrower scope.
examples.analytical: Biologists distinguish femaleness, defined by gametes and reproductive anatomy, from the social meanings that cultures attach to being a woman.

nuance.etymology: From female plus the suffix -ness, from Old English -nes.
common_mistakes: Using femaleness in everyday conversation where 'being a woman' or 'female' is more natural.
Stressing the final syllable, as in 'fee-mayl-NES.'

senses.definition: In a ferocious manner, particularly violent and aggressive.
Intensely or extremely.
senses.example: a ferociously fast pace

core.definition: In a fierce, violent or aggressive way, or with great intensity, as in 'ferociously competitive'.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ROH, the second syllable, and the 'ci' is pronounced 'sh'. The final -ly is a short 'lee', and the -ous ending reduces to 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in its basic sense of violence, but emphatic and positive when describing intense loyalty, humor or effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ferociously in news, sports and everyday talk, often for emphasis: 'She is ferociously organized.' It describes an animal or person attacking in the literal sense. It sounds more vivid than 'very', so it works well with friends, but it can sound overheated in a calm workplace.

distinctions.note: Fiercely is the more common and gentler choice for intensity, strong feeling or defense, while ferociously sounds more extreme.
Violently focuses on physical force and harm, whereas ferociously can describe wild energy or determination without violence.

examples.everyday: My little dog barks ferociously at the mail carrier, but he is really a big softie.
examples.professional: Our product teams compete ferociously for budget, so every planning meeting turns into a negotiation.
examples.analytical: Her argument is ferociously rigorous, dismantling each premise before she offers any conclusion of her own.

nuance.analogy: Ferociously works like a volume knob turned all the way up: the same action, but at maximum intensity.
nuance.etymology: From ferocious, from Latin ferox, ferocis, fierce, wild, plus -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable: fuh-ROH-shus-lee, not FER-oh-shus-lee.
Saying the second syllable as 'oh-see' instead of 'oh-shus'; the 'ci' is pronounced 'sh'.

senses.definition: In a fiery manner.

core.definition: In a passionate, intense or angry way, with great energy or heat.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the word has three syllables with a pronounced r after the middle vowel. Don't reduce it to two syllables like 'FYR-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests energy, passion or anger, depending on the verb it modifies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use fierily in everyday speech. They say 'passionately', 'heatedly' or 'with fiery passion' instead. You are most likely to see it in literary writing, sermons or historical description, while its root, fiery, is much more common in ordinary talk.

distinctions.note: Common and neutral about feeling; fierily adds a sense of visible heat or fire.
Used for arguing angrily; fierily can describe passion in speaking or defending, not only anger.
Means with strong force or aggression, not necessarily heat; fierily stresses fire and passion.

examples.professional: He defended the budget fierily, though the finance team was not convinced by his numbers.
examples.analytical: The prophet spoke fierily against injustice, and his words still provoke readers who study them closely.

nuance.analogy: Like a bonfire that burns hot and bright, the speaker gives off heat as well as light.
nuance.etymology: From fiery, from fire (Old English fȳr), with the adverb suffix -ly; the y changes to i before -ly.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'fierly' or 'fiercely'; the y changes to i before -ly, giving fierily.
Confusing it with 'fiercely', which means with strong force or aggression rather than fire.

senses.definition: Arrive; get to.
senses.example: I'm really puzzled at how this word salad managed to find its way into print.

core.definition: To manage to reach a place, often by navigating or by making your way through an unfamiliar situation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'way,' and 'one's' is weak and fast, sounding like 'wunz.' In natural speech the words link together, so 'find one's way' sounds almost like 'fyn-dwun-ZWAY.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'find one's way' for physically getting somewhere or for adjusting to a new job, school, or city. It is a friendly, everyday phrase, and it often describes a process that takes some time. A common reply is 'Let me know if you need help,' or 'You'll figure it out soon.'

distinctions.note: 'Get to' simply means arrive, while 'find one's way' suggests searching or effort to reach the place.
The two forms are interchangeable; 'one's' is more formal or impersonal, while 'your' is used in direct speech.

collocations: find your way to the office
find your way through the crowd
take time to find your way

examples.everyday: It took us almost an hour to find our way out of the parking garage the first time.
examples.professional: New engineers usually find their way around the codebase within a couple of weeks if they have a good mentor.
examples.analytical: The essay asks how a reader can find their way through the poem's shifting perspectives without losing the thread of its argument.

nuance.analogy: Finding one's way is like following a trail in the woods: each turn reveals the next step, until you arrive.
nuance.etymology: 'Find' from Old English findan; 'way' from Old English weg.
common_mistakes: Using 'find the way to' with a mismatched object, such as 'find my way to the store' when 'get to the store' would be simpler in casual speech.
Mixing up 'find one's way' with 'find the way,' which means locate a route rather than arrive.

senses.definition: A skill in the handling or manipulation of a situation.
The property of having elegance, grace, refinement, or skill.
senses.example: She handled the delicate negotiation with a finesse that impressed the whole board.

senses.definition: An adroit maneuver.
senses.example: His finesse in moving the vendor's price down without a fight saved us thousands.

senses.definition: In bridge, whist, etc.: a technique which allows one to win a trick, usually by playing a card when it is thought that a card that can beat it is held by another player whose turn is over.
senses.example: By leading the jack, South could try a finesse against the king in the opponent's hand.

senses.definition: To evade (a problem, situation, etc.) by using some clever argument or stratagem.
senses.example: The senator tried to finesse the question about the budget by changing the subject.

senses.definition: To handle or manage carefully or skilfully; to manipulate in a crafty way.
senses.example: The mediator finessed the two sides into agreeing to meet again next week.

senses.definition: To obtain something from someone through trickery or manipulation.
senses.example: He finessed a free upgrade out of the airline agent with a sad story.

senses.definition: To attempt to win a trick by finessing.
senses.example: Declarer decided to finesse rather than play for the drop in the suit.

senses.definition: To play (a card) as a finesse.
senses.example: East finessed the queen on the second round, hoping to pick up the trick.

core.definition: Skillful, subtle handling of a situation or task, often achieved with tact or cleverness rather than force.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable. The first syllable is a short, relaxed 'ih' sound, not 'fee'. The final s is a plain 's' sound, not 'z'.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing skill, tact, or elegance. Negative when used as a verb to mean evading rules or manipulating people through tricks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'handle it with finesse' or 'with real finesse' to praise someone who manages a delicate situation gracefully. As a verb, 'finesse' often suggests a clever workaround, sometimes slightly dishonest, so it can sound like criticism. In sports and business, the noun is common and positive; in casual talk, people usually say 'handled it smoothly' instead.

distinctions.note: Skill is the general ability to do something well; finesse adds a sense of subtlety, grace, and tact in handling delicate matters.
Tact is the ability to avoid offending people; finesse is broader and can include tactical cleverness and technical polish.
Force means using power or pressure; finesse means achieving the result through subtle, skillful methods.

examples.everyday: My sister handled that awkward phone call with real finesse, and nobody got upset.
examples.professional: The project manager showed finesse in calming the client without changing the deadline.
examples.analytical: Her argument displayed a philosophical finesse, distinguishing carefully between the two meanings of 'cause.'

nuance.analogy: Finesse is like a skilled dancer who guides a partner through a crowded floor without bumping anyone: smooth, precise, and nearly effortless.
nuance.etymology: From French 'finesse,' from 'fin' (fine), meaning delicacy or subtlety.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'NEE' instead of 'NES'.
Using 'finesse' as a synonym for 'finish' or 'fine quality' in technical product descriptions where 'refinement' is more natural.

finesse.etymology: From Middle English *finesse* (“a degree of excellence; fineness, purity”), from Middle French *finesse*, Old French *finesse* (“a fineness; a delicacy; slenderness”), from *fine*, *fin* (“fine, thin”) (from Latin *fīnis* (“an end”); compare ) + *-esse*.

senses.definition: Of a function, taking a finite number of arguments to produce an output.
senses.example: The proof relies on a finitary function that maps any finite list of integers to a single value.

senses.definition: Pertaining to finite-length proofs, each using a finite set of axioms.
senses.example: Hilbert hoped every mathematical claim could be verified through a finitary proof using only finitely many axioms.

core.definition: In mathematical logic, describing methods or proofs that use only finite objects and finitely many steps.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'tai' syllable is pronounced like 'tair,' with a clear American r, and the last syllable is a reduced 'ee'. Don't say 'FY-nih-tair-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional tone and is used only in specialized discussions.
nuance.usage_note: Finitary is a specialist term in logic, proof theory, and the foundations of mathematics, especially in discussions of Hilbert's program. Americans use it mainly in academic writing and lectures. In ordinary conversation, you would say 'using only finite methods' instead.

distinctions.note: Finite describes anything with a limited number; finitary specifically describes methods, proofs, or reasoning restricted to finite means.
Constructive proofs build objects explicitly and may use infinite processes in some frameworks; finitary proofs are a stricter subset limited to finite objects.

examples.everyday: My friend who studies logic said that some proofs are called finitary because they avoid infinite objects.
examples.professional: Our research group will check whether the algorithm's correctness argument stays within finitary methods.
examples.analytical: Hilbert hoped that a finitary proof could establish the consistency of arithmetic without appealing to infinite sets.

nuance.analogy: A finitary proof is like building a house using only materials you can count and hold in your hands, with no appeal to materials you cannot inspect.
nuance.etymology: From 'finite' with the suffix -ary, coined in mathematical logic in the 20th century.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'finitary' with 'finite,' which is a more general word.
Using 'finitary' to mean 'limited' in everyday contexts, where 'finite' or 'limited' is correct.

senses.definition: A reflexive jerking away.
senses.example: My eye doctor hates the flinch I have every time he tries to get near my eyes.

senses.definition: The slipping of the foot from a ball, when attempting to give a tight croquet.
senses.example: A sloppy flinch during the tight croquet shot sent his ball wide of the wicket.

senses.definition: To make a sudden, involuntary movement in response to a (usually negative) stimulus; to cringe; to blench.
To dodge (a question), to avoid an unpleasant task or duty.
senses.example: She flinched from the hard question about the budget and changed the subject.

senses.definition: To let the foot slip from a ball, when attempting to give a tight croquet.
senses.example: During the tight croquet shot, he flinched and let his foot slip off the ball.

core.definition: To make a sudden, involuntary movement of the body, usually away from something painful or frightening.

pronunciation.tip: It has one stressed syllable, FLINCH. The n is clearly pronounced before the ch, so do not drop it or add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can describe a natural reflex, or it can suggest a lack of courage when used about avoiding a task.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say flinch for a physical reaction, such as at a loud noise or a hard blow, and also for hesitating before an unpleasant task. Saying he did not flinch is a common way to praise someone's calm. In casual talk, people say they did not even flinch to mean they stayed calm.

distinctions.note: Cringe often describes embarrassment or disgust, while flinch describes a quick physical jerk away from something.
Wince is usually a grimace of pain, while flinch is a quicker movement that can happen without visible pain.

examples.everyday: The dentist was gentle, but I still flinched when the drill started.
examples.professional: I did not flinch when the client questioned the budget, because the numbers are solid.
examples.analytical: The author refuses to flinch from the moral consequences of the policy he defends.

nuance.analogy: Flinching is like your hand jerking off a hot stove before your brain has finished thinking.
nuance.etymology: From Old French flenchir, to bend or turn aside.
common_mistakes: Using flinch with a direct object as if it means avoid, such as flinch the question; say flinch from the question.
Pronouncing the final ch as a k sound.

flinch.etymology: From Middle French *flenchir* (“to bend”), from Old French *flenchir*, *flanchir*, from **hlankijan*, from Proto-Germanic **hlankijaną* (“to bend, twist, flex”), from Proto-Indo-European **kleng-* (“to bend, turn, wind”).

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, inhabiting, or produced by the action of a river or stream.
senses.example: The fluvial deposits along the riverbank contain sand and silt carried from upstream.

core.definition: Relating to rivers or streams, or formed by the flow and erosion of running water.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending is two light syllables, ee-uhl, and it should not sound like the word fluffy or like flu-vile.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fluvial in geology, geography, hydrology and environmental writing, often in the phrases fluvial erosion or fluvial deposits. In everyday talk they say river or stream instead. It is more formal than riverine, which usually describes an area or habitat beside a river.

distinctions.note: Riverine describes areas or habitats along a river, while fluvial describes processes caused by flowing water.
Alluvial describes deposits of sediment left by water, while fluvial covers the whole action of a river, including erosion and transport.
Lacustrine refers to lakes, while fluvial refers to rivers and streams.

examples.everyday: Walking along the creek, my neighbor pointed out the fluvial shaping of the banks after the spring floods.
examples.professional: The report attributes the downstream flooding to fluvial sediment that has built up over several years.
examples.analytical: Fluvial processes carve valleys over long timescales, and the landscape records that slow, patient work.

nuance.analogy: Like a sculptor who shapes stone with a chisel over centuries, a river carves and reshapes the land through fluvial erosion.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fluvialis, from fluvius, river, from fluere, to flow.
common_mistakes: Confusing fluvial, which means relating to rivers, with pluvial, which means relating to rain.
Pronouncing the word as flu-vee-al with a separate final a instead of a light uhl.

fluvial.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *fluviālis*, from *fluvius* + *ālis*, from the root of *fluo* (“to flow”).

senses.definition: A person with poor judgment or little intelligence.
senses.example: You were a fool to cross that busy road without looking.

senses.definition: A stock character typified by unintelligence, naïveté or lucklessness, usually as a form of comic relief; often used as a source of insight or pathos for the audience, as such characters are generally less bound by social expectations.
senses.example: The fool in the play gets the most honest lines, since nobody expects him to follow the rules.

senses.definition: Someone who has been made a fool of or tricked; dupe.
senses.example: Everyone at the office saw him as the fool who wired money to the fake lawyer.

senses.definition: Someone who derives pleasure from something specified.
senses.example: She is a fool for late-night pizza and never refuses a slice.

senses.definition: An informal greeting akin to buddy, dude, or man.
senses.example: Hey, fool, you finally made it to practice on time today!

senses.definition: A particular card in a tarot deck, representing a jester.
senses.example: In the tarot reading, the Fool card suggested a risky new beginning.

senses.definition: A type of dessert made of puréed fruit and custard or cream.
senses.example: an apricot fool; a gooseberry fool

senses.definition: (historical) A jester; a person whose role was to entertain a sovereign and the court (or lower personages).
senses.example: The king laughed loudly at the jester, his fool, who mocked the nobles at dinner.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To trick; to deceive.
senses.example: Don't let the salesman fool you with those fine print promises.

senses.definition: To act in an idiotic manner; to act foolishly.
senses.example: Stop fooling around with that ladder before you hurt yourself.

senses.definition: Foolish.
senses.example: Honestly, that was a fool decision for a man with two kids.

core.definition: A person who lacks good judgment or sense and does silly or unwise things.

pronunciation.tip: A single syllable with a long oo vowel and a dark l at the end. Don't add a vowel after the l, as in 'fool-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and mildly insulting when used about a person. In set phrases like 'April Fool' or 'play the fool' it can be playful.
nuance.usage_note: Calling someone a fool is harsh and can sound personal or rude, so Americans often choose softer words such as 'that was a mistake' or 'a little silly.' The exclamation 'You fool!' sounds dramatic or old-fashioned. Common set phrases include 'make a fool of yourself,' 'fool's errand,' and 'Fool me once, shame on you.'

distinctions.note: Idiot is stronger and more insulting; fool is milder and can be playful or affectionate.
A jester was a historical entertainer paid to make people laugh; a fool is someone who acts unwisely.
A dupe is someone who is deliberately tricked; a fool may simply lack judgment, with no trickery involved.

examples.everyday: Don't be a fool, call a cab before you drive home tonight.
examples.professional: I was a fool to skip the code review, and we shipped a bug that broke checkout.
examples.analytical: The wise person and the fool are contrasted throughout the wisdom literature as two ways of living.

nuance.analogy: A fool is like someone who keeps touching a hot stove after being burned: the lesson is obvious, yet ignored.
nuance.etymology: From Old French fol, from Late Latin follis, meaning bellows or windbag.
common_mistakes: Saying 'make fool of' without the article; the correct phrase is 'make a fool of'.
Using fool as an everyday adjective; say 'foolish' (fool is almost always a noun or verb in modern English).
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the Hebrew nabal names a morally deficient person who rejects God and wisdom, and the Greek moros denotes foolishness, as in 1 Corinthians. Psalm 14:1 (RSV) says the fool says in his heart that there is no God, which shows that the fool's problem is moral as well as intellectual. Proverbs 1:7 (RSV) teaches that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, while fools despise wisdom and instruction. 1 Corinthians 1:18-25 describes the message of the cross as foolishness to those who are perishing and says that God's foolishness is wiser than human wisdom.

fool.etymology: From Middle English *fol* (“fool”), from Old French *fol* from Latin *follis*.

senses.definition: Synonym of for the time being.

core.definition: Temporarily; for now, for a limited period until things change. A shorter, less common form of 'for the time being'.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce the r in 'for' clearly, and say 'thuh' with a soft th before the consonant; in fast speech 'for' reduces toward 'fer'. The stress falls on TIME, and the r is kept, unlike in many British accents.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly bookish; the short form sounds old-fashioned or written in conversation, so it can seem stiff.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this short form in speech. They normally say 'for now' in casual talk or 'for the time being' in more careful speech. You will meet 'for the time' in older novels, formal writing and some British texts, so recognize it but prefer the fuller phrase.

distinctions.note: The fuller and more common form; use it instead of the short version in everyday American English.
Casual and very common in speech; it suggests a temporary state that may change soon.

examples.everyday: Our Wi-Fi is down, so let's use my phone's hotspot for the time.
examples.professional: The vendor will host the reports on our old server for the time, since the new system isn't ready.
examples.analytical: For the time, the author's argument rests on an assumption it never defends, which leaves the conclusion provisional.

nuance.analogy: Like a temporary bridge: it carries traffic for now but was never meant to be the permanent road.
nuance.etymology: Built from the prepositional phrase 'for the time', meaning for a period of time; it is a shortened form of 'for the time being'.
common_mistakes: Using the short form 'for the time' in casual speech, where Americans say 'for now' or 'for the time being'.
Dropping the r in 'for' (saying something like 'faw'), which sounds British and can blur the phrase for American listeners.

senses.definition: The ability, or the due use of one's ability, to foresee or prepare wisely for the future.
senses.example: Having the foresight to prepare an evacuation plan may have saved their lives.

senses.definition: The ability to foresee future events in a supernatural or paranormal way, such as psychically.
senses.example: The fortune-teller claimed her foresight came from visions that no one else could see.

senses.definition: The front sight on a firearm (e.g. rifle, handgun).
senses.example: Align the rear sight with the foresight before you squeeze the trigger on the rifle.

senses.definition: A bearing taken forwards towards a new object.
senses.example: The navigator took a foresight on the lighthouse before plotting our course.

core.definition: The ability to think ahead and prepare wisely for future events and problems.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FOR. The second syllable is a one-syllable 'sight', so the word has two syllables. Do not split the ending into 'sigh-ut'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's wise planning and ability to avoid problems.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'foresight' to praise someone who planned ahead, as in 'She had the foresight to back up the files'. It is common in business and everyday speech. Be careful: 'foresight' does not mean that you knew something would happen; it means you prepared wisely.

distinctions.note: 'Hindsight' is understanding of past events after they happen; 'foresight' is planning before events happen.
'Insight' is a deep understanding of a situation or person; 'foresight' is specifically about the future.

examples.everyday: Thanks for bringing an umbrella; that was good foresight, since it started raining right after lunch.
examples.professional: The team's foresight in building redundancy into the database saved us during last month's outage.
examples.analytical: Her foresight lies not in predicting exact outcomes but in recognizing which risks deserve preparation now.

nuance.analogy: Like checking the weather before a hike: you prepare for what might come.
nuance.etymology: From 'fore' (before) plus 'sight' (seeing).
common_mistakes: Using 'foresight' to mean an intuition or prophecy, which is a different sense.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'sigh-ut' instead of one syllable 'sight'.

foresight.etymology: From Middle English *forsight*, *forsyght*, *forsichte* (since 14th c.), a calque of Latin *providentia*.

senses.definition: Getting your cup filled again at no extra charge, common for soda and coffee in the US.
senses.example: Our diner offers a free refill on coffee, so I always order a large.

core.definition: A second or later filling of your drink, such as soda or coffee, given at no extra charge at a restaurant.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on REE in refill, and free has a lighter secondary stress. Refill has a long ee in the first syllable and a short i in the second, so it is not refill with a long i ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It sounds friendly and helpful, and people usually appreciate it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say free refill in restaurants, diners, and fast food places when asking for another cup of soda or coffee. It is common in casual dining, and servers often ask, Would you like a free refill? A natural request is Can I get a free refill, please? Some places charge for refills, so ask if you are unsure.

distinctions.note: Top off means filling a glass to the top, often during a meal, and does not necessarily mean a second drink at no charge.
Second cup is a simpler request for another drink, but it does not indicate that the refill is free.

examples.everyday: Can I get a free refill on my iced tea, please?
examples.professional: Let's grab lunch at the diner, and they usually give a free refill on coffee.
examples.analytical: A free refill policy reduces the marginal cost of a customer's second drink, which is why restaurants use it to encourage longer visits.

nuance.analogy: A free refill is like a friendly host who keeps your glass full without asking you to pay for every sip.
nuance.etymology: Free from Old English freo, meaning not bound or without cost; refill from re- and fill.
common_mistakes: Saying refill with a long i in the second syllable.
Assuming every drink refill is free in all restaurants, when some places charge.
Using free refill for food; it is normally used for drinks.

conversation.text: Do you guys do free refills on soda here?
Coffee comes with free refills, so take your time.
I love this diner because they give you free refills on iced tea.

senses.definition: To cause to feel fear; to scare; to cause to feel alarm or fright.
senses.example: Avery puts a sheet over her head, pretending to be a ghost to frighten Emily.

senses.definition: To become scared or alarmed.
senses.example: Honestly, I don't frighten easily, so the loud thunder barely bothered me.

core.definition: To make someone feel afraid or suddenly scared.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on FRY. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so the word has two syllables, not three; the 'en' sounds like 'uhn.'

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, depending on context. It describes an unpleasant feeling caused by something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frighten for both sudden shock and longer-lasting fear. It is common in everyday speech, especially in phrases like 'you scared me' or 'that frightened me.' Saying 'You frightened me!' after a surprise is natural, and a common reply is 'Sorry, I didn't mean to.'

distinctions.note: Scare is more informal and is very common in American speech. Frighten is slightly more formal or descriptive.
Terrify means to cause intense fear. Frighten can describe milder fear.

examples.everyday: You frightened me when you came in without knocking.
examples.professional: The sudden outage frightened the team, but the on-call engineer calmed everyone down quickly.
examples.analytical: The text asks whether a demanding God is meant to frighten believers or to draw them toward moral seriousness.

nuance.analogy: To frighten someone is like flipping a light switch in a dark room: the sudden change makes you jump.
nuance.etymology: From fright, from Old English fyrhto, plus the verb suffix -en.
common_mistakes: Using frighten as a noun; the noun is fright.
Confusing frightened (feeling afraid) with frightening (causing fear).
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible frequently speaks of fear and of being frightened. In the Old Testament, the Hebrew verb yare' means to fear or be afraid, and it can refer to dread of danger or reverent awe toward God. In the New Testament, the Greek word phobeō carries similar meanings, from ordinary fright to reverence. Isaiah 41:10 offers God's assurance to Israel that he will strengthen and help them, so they need not be dismayed. Matthew 10:28 teaches that disciples should not fear those who can kill the body, but fear the one who can destroy both soul and body. Mark 6:50 describes the disciples being terrified at seeing Jesus walk on the sea, and Jesus calming them.

senses.definition: (archaic) A person's given name.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: A person's given name, the first name before the family name. This term is rare; Americans normally say first name or given name.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FRONT, then give name a clear long a. The word is rare, so 'first name' is usually the better choice in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It has no emotional charge, but it sounds unusual to most Americans and may cause confusion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say first name in everyday speech and given name on forms, in formal writing, or when discussing naming customs in other cultures. Front name is so uncommon that many native speakers would not recognize it as a standard term. Use first name to avoid confusion.

distinctions.note: First name is the everyday American term; front name is rare and may puzzle listeners.
Given name is more formal and is used on forms or in cultural discussions where name order differs.

examples.everyday: Can I get your first name for the reservation?
examples.professional: Please enter your legal first name exactly as it appears on your passport.
examples.analytical: Translators must decide whether the given name or the family name appears first in a Chinese or Korean record.

nuance.analogy: Like the name on the top line of a sign-in sheet, the one that comes before your family name.
nuance.etymology: Compound of front and name; the sense for a given name is rare in English and is recorded mainly in dictionaries.
common_mistakes: Asking for a 'front name' on a form; write 'first name' instead.
Confusing front name with last name, since the word front might suggest the opposite of back or end.

senses.definition: US standard spelling of fulfilment.
senses.example: Teaching young students gave him a deep fulfillment he never found in consulting.

core.definition: The completion of something required or promised, or the deep feeling of satisfaction that comes from achieving what matters to you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FIL, the second syllable. The last syllable is weak, like 'munt', not a strong 'ment' with a full vowel. Avoid saying three equal syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests completion, achievement, and a sense of meaning, and it is often used in personal and professional contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans spell this word 'fulfillment' with one 'l' after 'fill' and one 'l' before 'ment', while the British 'fulfilment' is not used in US writing. In casual speech, Americans often talk about 'finding fulfillment' in a job, relationship, or faith. The word can also be formal, as in 'the fulfillment of a contract'.

distinctions.note: Satisfaction is more immediate and often about pleasure or meeting a need; fulfillment suggests a deeper, longer sense of purpose.
Success means achieving a goal, while fulfillment includes the personal meaning and contentment that come with it.
Completion is the act of finishing something; fulfillment includes the sense that the completion matters personally or morally.

examples.everyday: Teaching my kids to ride bikes gave me a real sense of fulfillment this summer.
examples.professional: Our team tracks customer fulfillment rates to measure how many orders are delivered on time.
examples.analytical: Aquinas describes human fulfillment as the vision of God, the end toward which the whole human person is directed.

nuance.analogy: Fulfillment is like a garden that has finally bloomed after a long season of care.
nuance.etymology: From fulfill, with the suffix -ment, meaning the act or state of fulfilling.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling 'fulfilment' in American writing.
Confusing it with 'fulfilling', the adjective, as in 'a fulfilling job', when you need the noun 'fulfillment'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, fulfillment often refers to God completing his promises in history. Matthew 1:22 describes events that fulfill what was spoken by the prophets, and the Greek noun plērōma, meaning fullness or completion, appears in Ephesians 1:23 for the church as the fullness of Christ.

senses.definition: A gas or vapor/vapor that is strong-smelling or dangerous to inhale.
senses.example: Don't stand around in there breathing the fumes while the adhesive cures.

senses.definition: A material that has been vaporized from the solid or liquid state to the gas state and re-coalesced to the solid state.
senses.example: Lead fume is a grayish powder, mainly comprising lead sulfate.

senses.definition: Rage or excitement which deprives the mind of self-control.
senses.example: In a fume, he slammed the door and stormed out of the meeting.

senses.definition: Anything unsubstantial or airy; idle conceit; vain imagination.
senses.example: His grand plans for the startup were nothing but fumes of vanity.

senses.definition: The incense of praise; inordinate flattery.
senses.example: The courtier drowned the king in fumes of flattery at every banquet.

senses.definition: To expose (something) to fumes; specifically, to expose wood, etc. to ammonia in order to produce dark tints.
senses.example: The woodworker fumed the oak cabinet in ammonia to deepen its color.

senses.definition: To apply or offer incense to.
senses.example: The priest fumed the altar with frankincense before the Easter procession.

senses.definition: To emit fumes.
senses.example: The old diesel truck fumed in the parking lot while the driver waited.

senses.definition: To pass off in fumes or vapors.
senses.example: Her irritation fumed off within minutes, leaving only a tired sigh behind.

senses.definition: To express or feel great anger.
senses.example: He’s still fuming about the argument they had yesterday.

senses.definition: To be as in a mist; to be dulled and stupefied.
senses.example: After the long sermon, the congregation sat fumed and drowsy in the heat.

core.definition: A gas or vapor, often strong-smelling or harmful to breathe, such as exhaust or paint fumes.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the stress on the vowel, pronounced 'fyoom', not 'foom' or 'fyoo-may'. Americans usually say the plural 'fumes' most often.

nuance.connotation: Negative: fumes usually suggest something unpleasant or dangerous to breathe, such as car exhaust or chemical odors.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fumes' constantly for car exhaust, gasoline, paint, cleaning products, and smoke from a stove or grill. Saying 'Can you open a window? The paint fumes are strong' is very natural. The rage sense ('in a fume') is old-fashioned, so in everyday speech Americans say 'fuming' or 'fired up' instead.

distinctions.note: Smoke is the visible cloud of particles from burning; fumes are gases or vapors, often invisible, and are usually sharp-smelling.
Vapor is a neutral word for any gas or mist, such as water vapor; fumes implies a strong smell and possible harm.
An odor is any smell; fumes are specifically gases that you inhale and that can be dangerous.

examples.everyday: Can you open a window? The paint fumes are really strong in here.
examples.professional: The facilities team said the solvent fumes from the lab must be vented before the next shift starts.
examples.analytical: Early chemists often treated the fumes of burning sulfur as evidence of a hidden, invisible substance.

nuance.analogy: Fumes are like an invisible smell that you breathe in, and it can make you sick.
nuance.etymology: From Old French fum, from Latin fumus, meaning smoke.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'foom' (as in 'zoom') instead of 'fyoom'.
Using 'fume' as a countable noun in everyday speech; Americans usually say 'fumes' in the plural.

fume.etymology: From Middle English *fume*, from Old French *fum* (“smoke, steam, vapour”), from Latin *fūmus* (“vapour, smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European **dʰuh₂mós* (“smoke”), from **dʰewh₂-* (“to smoke, raise dust”).

senses.definition: Strange or unusual, often in an unpleasant way.
senses.example: The milk smelt funny so I poured it away.

senses.definition: Amusing; humorous; comical.
senses.example: I know you'll enjoy chatting with her — she's really funny and smart.

senses.definition: A joke.
senses.example: Dad always sprung a funny at dinner, usually something terrible.

senses.definition: A comic strip.
senses.example: The Sunday newspaper's funny about the office printer always made me laugh.

senses.definition: Humor in general.
senses.example: Where's the funny? Your meme sucks.

core.definition: Amusing or humorous; likely to make you laugh.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, FUH. The vowel is short, like the u in 'cup', not the oo in 'fun' said slowly; the final -y is a clear 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it means amusing, but neutral or negative when it means strange or suspicious, as in 'something funny is going on'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use funny constantly in casual talk to describe jokes, movies, and people with a good sense of humor. Be careful: 'funny' can also mean strange or suspicious, so 'That noise is funny' sounds like a worry, not a joke. For a polite, more formal description of humor, Americans might say 'amusing' or 'witty'. A natural reply to a joke is 'Ha, that's funny!' or 'Very funny.' (Said sarcastically, 'Very funny' means the joke was not good.)

distinctions.note: Humorous is more formal and literary; funny is the everyday word.
Amusing is milder and suggests mild entertainment; funny suggests making you laugh out loud.

examples.everyday: That movie was so funny that I was still laughing on the drive home.
examples.professional: Someone on the call made a funny comment about our quarterly numbers, and it broke the tension in the meeting.
examples.analytical: Hobbes suggested that laughter arises from a sudden sense of superiority, so what makes a joke funny may depend on who it targets.

nuance.analogy: Funny is like a good spark of light in a room: it brightens the mood instantly.
nuance.etymology: From fun, with the suffix -y, meaning 'full of fun'.
common_mistakes: Using 'funny' to mean 'fun' in a positive sense, e.g. 'We had a funny time', which sounds odd to Americans; say 'We had a lot of fun'.
Saying 'funny' for a strange noise or smell without realizing it may sound alarming.

conversation.text: Your brother is so funny. I couldn't stop laughing.
Have you seen any funny movies lately?
That's funny; I thought I left my keys right here.
This milk smells funny. When did we buy it?

senses.definition: Any trench, channel, or groove; often found on wood or metal.
senses.example: Don't walk across that deep furrow in the field.

senses.definition: A trench cut in the soil, as when plowed in order to plant a crop.
senses.example: Don't walk across that deep furrow in the field.

senses.definition: A deep wrinkle in the skin of the face, especially on the forehead.
senses.example: When she was tired, a deep furrow appeared on her forehead.

senses.definition: To cut one or more grooves in (the ground, etc.).
senses.example: Cart wheels can furrow roads.

senses.definition: To wrinkle.
senses.example: She began to furrow her brow as the numbers in the report failed to add up.

senses.definition: To pull one's brows or eyebrows together due to concentration, worry, etc.
senses.example: As she pored over the company's bewildering tax documents, she furrowed her brows, wrinkled her nose, and began to frown her befuddlement.

senses.definition: To become furrowed.
senses.example: His forehead began to furrow as he read the disappointing test results.

core.definition: A narrow groove cut into the soil by a plow, or a deep wrinkle in the skin, especially on the forehead.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FUR, and the second syllable is 'oh', a diphthong. Do not say the British-style 'FUH-roh' with an 'uh' vowel; the American form uses the 'er' vowel in 'fur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in farming contexts; negative or serious when describing worry on a face.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'furrow' in farming to describe the groove a plow makes in a field, as in 'The farmer followed the furrow.' In everyday talk, people say 'wrinkle' or 'crease', but 'furrowed brow' is a common phrase for someone who is worried or concentrating. The verb 'furrow your brow' is natural in casual speech. The word can also describe a groove cut into wood or metal.

distinctions.note: A wrinkle is any fold in the skin; a furrow is a deeper, more pronounced line, often from worry or age.
A groove is any narrow channel; a furrow usually refers to a channel cut in soil by a plow.

examples.everyday: You're furrowing your brow again, so what's bothering you?
examples.professional: Before the meeting, the manager furrowed his brow at the spreadsheet, which made everyone nervous.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard often describes anxiety as a furrow cut deep into the self, a mark left by repeated reflection on one's own choices.

nuance.analogy: A furrow is like a path worn into a face or field: the same movement, repeated, leaves a lasting line.
nuance.etymology: From Old English furh, 'furrow, trench'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'FUH-roh' with an 'uh' vowel, which is not standard in American English.
Using 'furrow' for any wrinkle; the word is best for deeper lines, especially on the forehead.

furrow.etymology: From Middle English *forow*, *furgh*, from Old English *furh*, from **furh*, from Proto-Germanic **furhs*, from Proto-Indo-European **perḱ-* (“to dig”).

senses.definition: Football (soccer)

core.definition: Soccer, the sport in which teams try to score by kicking a round ball into a goal, mostly without using their hands.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is 'bahl' with the open vowel of cot, not the 'bowl' or 'ball' sound of Standard British speech. Avoid stressing the -bol.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a sport and is used with warmth in Spanish-speaking communities and among fans.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans say soccer for this sport. Futbol, from Spanish, is used by Spanish speakers, in Spanish-language media, and by many fans who want to show their cultural background. In the United States, football means American football, so saying football for soccer can confuse people.

distinctions.note: Soccer is the standard American English word; futbol is mainly used by Spanish speakers or in Spanish-language contexts.
In American English, football means American football, a different sport with different rules and equipment.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's kids play futbol every Saturday at the park down the street.
examples.professional: Our marketing team sponsors a local futbol league for kids in the area.
examples.analytical: In the United States the sport carries different names, soccer for some and futbol for others, and each name signals a community.

nuance.analogy: The same ball and the same game, but the name you use tells people who you are and where you grew up.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish fútbol, borrowed from English football.
common_mistakes: Using futbol to mean American football, which causes confusion in the United States.
Stressing the second syllable, as in foot-BOHL, instead of the first.

senses.definition: To decorate with ornaments; to adorn; to embellish.
senses.example: The bakers garnished the cakes with candied violets and gold leaf for the wedding.

senses.definition: To ornament with something placed around it.
senses.example: a dish garnished with a sprig/spray of parsley

senses.definition: To warn by garnishment; to give notice to.
senses.example: The creditor's lawyer garnished the bank, giving it formal notice of the pending claim.

senses.definition: To have (money) set aside by court order (particularly for the payment of alleged debts); to garnishee.
senses.example: After he ignored the judgment, the court garnished his wages to cover the unpaid loan.

senses.definition: A set of dishes, often pewter, containing a dozen pieces of several types.
senses.example: Grandmother's dining room cabinet held a full pewter garnish, twelve pieces gleaming on the shelves.

senses.definition: Pewter vessels in general.
senses.example: The antique shop sold old English garnish, mostly plates and tankards in dull silver tones.

senses.definition: Something added for embellishment.
senses.example: Her plain pasta was transformed by a garnish of fresh basil and shaved parmesan.

senses.definition: Clothes; garments, especially when showy or decorative.
senses.example: Look at your garnish, Tom, you'll never pass for a gentleman.

senses.definition: Something set round or upon a dish as an embellishment.
senses.example: The chef set a sprig of mint and a thin lemon slice as garnish beside the lamb.

senses.definition: Cash.
senses.example: He patted his pockets, hunting for enough garnish to pay the cab driver.

senses.definition: (historical) A fee; specifically, in English jails, formerly an unauthorized fee demanded from a newcomer by the older prisoners.
senses.example: In the old county jail, newcomers paid a garnish to the older prisoners or faced rough treatment.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: To decorate food by adding small amounts of herbs, fruit, or other ingredients on or around it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, GAR. The r is strongly pronounced, and the -ish ending sounds like 'fish,' with no extra vowel between n and sh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical or decorative action in cooking or service.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use garnish in restaurants and cooking, such as garnish with parsley or a lemon wedge. A garnish is small and decorative, not a side dish, so if you want more food, ask for a side. In legal and payroll talk, garnish wages means that a court orders money taken from paychecks.

distinctions.note: Decorate is general and can apply to any object, while garnish is specific to food or drink.
A side is an extra food served with the main dish, while a garnish is a small decorative addition.

examples.everyday: Can you garnish my iced tea with a lemon slice, please?
examples.professional: The chef wants to garnish each plate with microgreens so the presentation looks consistent.
examples.analytical: To garnish a dish is to add something that changes its appearance more than its substance, which raises questions about where decoration ends and content begins.

nuance.analogy: Like a painter adding a few final brushstrokes to a finished canvas, changing how it looks without changing the structure.
nuance.etymology: From Old French garnir, 'to equip, furnish, or warn,' of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Calling a side dish a garnish; a garnish is small and decorative, while a side is an extra portion.
Using garnish as a verb with the wrong preposition; say garnish with parsley, not garnish by parsley.

conversation.text: Add a sprig of mint as a garnish.
The garnish is just for looks; you don't have to eat it.
She garnished the soup with fresh parsley.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being gelid.

core.definition: The quality of being extremely cold or icy, a bitter chill that seems to freeze the surroundings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, LID. The first syllable is a weak juh, and the t between vowels is usually flapped in American speech, so it sounds close to a quick d. The word ends in a light ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes bitter cold or an emotionally frozen manner, and it is more vivid than coldness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use gelidity in casual speech; they say the cold or the chill instead. You will meet it in literary criticism, nature writing, weather descriptions with a formal tone, or when describing a frozen stare or manner. Gelid is the adjective, and a native speaker may say 'gelid' in writing when they want a sharp, elegant contrast to warm.

distinctions.note: Coldness is the everyday word for lack of warmth; gelidity is rarer and suggests an icy, almost lifeless chill.
Frigidity can mean extreme cold, but in modern English it is mostly used for sexual unresponsiveness, so it can be misread.
A chill is a cold feeling, often temporary, while gelidity describes a deeper, more absolute cold.

collocations: the gelidity of the night air

examples.professional: The sensor logs show the cold storage room hit a gelidity that exceeded the safe limit for the samples overnight.
examples.analytical: The poem's gelidity is rhetorical rather than meteorological: its chill signals death and emotional distance, not a drop in temperature.

nuance.analogy: Like a frozen lake that looks still and beautiful but hides a cold that no one can survive for long.
nuance.etymology: From Latin gelidus 'icy, cold', from gelu 'frost', with the English suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as a long i, as in LIE-did-ity.
Using gelidity in casual conversation where cold or chill is more natural.
Confusing it with frigidity, which has a different and sometimes sexual meaning in modern use.

senses.definition: Throughout a genome.
senses.example: We scanned the samples genome-wide to find variants linked to early-onset diabetes.

senses.definition: Throughout a genome.
senses.example: We scanned the samples genome-wide to find variants linked to early-onset diabetes.

core.definition: Covering or analyzing the entire genome of an organism, rather than only selected genes or regions.

pronunciation.tip: The first part, JEE-nohm, carries the strongest stress, and 'wide' is a lighter secondary stress. Don't reduce the 'o' in 'genome' to an 'uh' sound; it is a clear 'oh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical description of scope.
nuance.usage_note: Used mainly in genetics, genomics, biomedical research, and data science, often before nouns such as study or association. In labs and papers you will see the full phrase 'genome-wide association study', which Americans shorten to GWAS. For a general audience, people say 'across the whole genome' instead.

distinctions.note: Genomic is a broad term for anything relating to the genome; genome-wide specifically means covering the entire genome, not a selected part.
A targeted analysis examines chosen genes or regions, while a genome-wide analysis scans the whole genome without preselecting.

examples.everyday: The lab said their test is genome-wide, so it checks your whole DNA instead of just a few genes.
examples.professional: We'll run a genome-wide association study on the cohort and correct for population structure.
examples.analytical: A genome-wide approach avoids the bias of choosing candidate genes in advance, though it creates a severe multiple-testing problem.

nuance.analogy: It is like proofreading a whole book instead of checking only the chapter you already suspect has typos.
nuance.etymology: Combines genome, from German Genom, coined in 1920 from gene and chromosome, with the English word wide.
common_mistakes: Dropping the hyphen in writing; the compound is standardly written with a hyphen before a noun.
Using genome-wide for a single gene or small region, which is the opposite of its meaning.

senses.definition: To interact or coexist well, without argument or trouble.
senses.example: I wish the kids would get along better.

senses.definition: To survive; to do well enough.
senses.example: She didn’t have a lot of money, but she had enough to get along.

senses.definition: To go; to move; to leave.
senses.example: Driver, get along there.

core.definition: To have a friendly relationship with someone, without serious conflict.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'long'. The 'ng' is one sound, so do not add a 'g' after it. In speech, 'get along' links as 'ge-tuh-LAWNG'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes a harmonious relationship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for people such as coworkers, roommates or family members who get on well: 'Do you two get along?' It is casual and very common. Get on is more typical of British English, so Americans would normally use get along. A natural reply is 'We get along great.'

distinctions.note: Get on is more typical of British English, while Americans prefer get along for relationships.
Agree means having the same opinion; get along means having a good relationship even when you disagree.

examples.everyday: My sister and I get along better now that we're both older.
examples.professional: Our new team members get along well, so we can focus on the release.
examples.analytical: The thesis asks whether pluralist societies can get along without a shared account of the good.

nuance.analogy: Like two dancers who keep in step, people who get along move together without tripping over each other.
common_mistakes: Saying 'get along to' instead of 'get along with' when naming a person.
Using it for a single moment of agreement; it describes an ongoing relationship.

conversation.text: I get along really well with my coworkers.
Do your kids get along with each other?
How are you getting along in your new apartment?
My kids get along really well most of the time.

senses.definition: To inflict trouble or harm on another in return, typically the same as that inflicted on oneself.
senses.example: After she sabotaged my presentation, I vowed to get even at the next meeting.

core.definition: To take revenge by doing something harmful back to someone who harmed you.
