examples.analytical: Some of the repeated arguments in the chapter run on so monotonously that the central claim gets lost.

nuance.analogy: Speaking monotonously is like a metronome ticking the same beat for an hour; it never changes.
nuance.etymology: From Greek monotonos 'single-toned', from monos 'single' and tonos 'tone', with -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with monotonically, which is the mathematical term.
Stressing the first syllable, as in MAH-nuh-tun-us-lee; the stress belongs on NAH.

senses.definition: One who mops (uses a mop).
senses.example: The night-shift mopper finished the hallway floors before the first patients arrived.

senses.definition: One who mops (makes grimaces).
senses.example: moppers and mowers

core.definition: A person who cleans floors with a mop, especially someone whose job or regular task is mopping.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final er is a reduced rhotic syllable, so the r is clearly pronounced in American speech. Do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a cleaning task and carries no judgment, though the job itself is often undervalued.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use mopper as a job title; they more often say custodian, janitor or cleaner. The word appears mainly in descriptions of a literal activity, such as a night mopper who cleans the floors after the store closes. Be careful, because mopper is easily confused with moper, a person who mopes.

distinctions.note: A janitor is a broader term for a building worker who does many cleaning and maintenance tasks, while a mopper specifically cleans floors with a mop.
Custodian is a more formal, institutional term, often used for school or government building staff, and covers more duties than mopping.
A moper is a person who sulks or mopes, while a mopper is someone who cleans floors with a mop.

examples.everyday: The mopper already came through the kitchen, so the floor is still wet, so please walk around it.
examples.professional: We need a mopper on the night shift to keep the lobby floors clean before the morning crowd arrives.
examples.analytical: The mopper's work is invisible until it is missing, which is why cleaning labor is so often overlooked in economic analysis.

nuance.analogy: A mopper is like the quiet stagehand of a building: nobody notices until the floor is dirty, and then everyone notices.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the verb mop, from Middle English mappe, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing mopper, someone who cleans with a mop, with moper, someone who mopes.
Using mopper as a formal job title in American workplaces, where custodian or janitor is more typical.

senses.definition: Without mortar.

core.definition: Built or set without mortar, the paste that holds bricks or stones together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOR, and keep the ending -less short and light, like the word less. Use the vowel of more, not the vowel of mow.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical description of construction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mortarless mainly in construction, masonry and archaeology, as in mortarless stone walls. In everyday talk people say dry-stacked or built without mortar. The word is clear but rarely used outside technical writing.

distinctions.note: Dry-stacked is the more common American term in construction for stones set without mortar.
Unmortared means the same thing but is less common in American writing.

examples.everyday: The stone wall in our backyard is mortarless, so you can see the small gaps between the rocks.
examples.professional: The contractor specified a mortarless design for the retaining wall so that water can drain through it.
examples.analytical: The mortarless walls of the ancient site show a precision that scholars still debate, since the builders left no binding material behind.

nuance.analogy: Like a jigsaw puzzle held together only by the shape of its pieces.
nuance.etymology: From mortar plus the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel like mow
Confusing it with mortal or morals

senses.definition: Abbreviation of Mister.
Abbreviation of March.

core.definition: Courtesy title written before a man's surname or full name, short for 'Mister'. Written as Mr. with a period.

pronunciation.tip: Americans say the full word 'mister,' not the letters M-R. Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -er is a light, reduced American r-sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite; it signals respect in formal or business settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Mr. before a man's last name in writing, introductions and formal address, such as 'Mr. Garcia' or 'Mr. Chen.' In casual speech people often drop the title and use first names. Use Mr. only before a surname or full name, never before a first name alone. Mr. is an abbreviation, so the American style includes a period, as in 'Mr. Lee.'

distinctions.note: Mister is the full spelled-out form, used when speaking aloud or in formal writing; Mr. is the abbreviation used in most written contexts.
Mrs. is the title for a married woman, while Mr. is used for men regardless of marital status.

examples.everyday: Hi, is Mr. Lee around? I'm returning his casserole dish.
examples.professional: Mr. Patel will present the Q3 results at two o'clock, so please hold your questions until the end.
examples.analytical: The committee minutes record Mr. Johnson's objection, which the board never fully addressed in its final report.

nuance.analogy: Like a name badge on a man's name: it tells you his role of respect before you even know him well.
nuance.etymology: Short for Mister, a reduced form of master.
common_mistakes: Saying the letters 'em-ar' instead of 'mister'.
Using Mr. before a first name only, as in 'Mr. John' instead of 'Mr. Smith' or 'John'.

senses.definition: Any material used to cover the top layer of soil to protect, insulate, or decorate it, or to discourage weeds or retain moisture.
senses.example: An organic mulch is a mulch made of natural substances such as leaves or grass clippings.

senses.definition: To apply mulch.
senses.example: Mulch your vegetable garden to retain moisture and keep weeds down.

senses.definition: To turn into mulch.
senses.example: I decided to mulch the grass clippings.

core.definition: Material such as bark, straw or compost spread over soil to hold moisture, block weeds or protect plants.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a short u, as in 'cup'. The l is clear, and the ch is a single sound, not 'mulsh' or 'mul-chuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a practical gardening term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mulch constantly in home gardening, especially for flower beds and tree rings in spring. Garden centers sell bags of wood-chip or bark mulch, and gardening advice often says to mulch to keep soil moist. As a verb, mulch is common in everyday talk: 'I need to mulch the beds this weekend.'

distinctions.note: Compost is decayed organic matter mixed into soil to feed it; mulch is spread on top to cover and protect the soil.
Fertilizer adds nutrients to soil, while mulch mainly conserves moisture and blocks weeds.

examples.everyday: I put a thick layer of mulch around the roses to keep the weeds out.
examples.professional: Our landscaping crew mulches the parking-lot islands in April so the plants keep moisture through the summer.
examples.analytical: Mulch reduces soil temperature swings and evaporation, which explains its central role in drought-tolerant landscape design.

nuance.analogy: Mulch is like a blanket on a sleeping child: it keeps the ground warm, moist and protected.
common_mistakes: Confusing mulch with compost; compost is mixed into soil, while mulch sits on top.
Piling mulch against tree trunks, which can cause rot; keep it a few inches away from the trunk.

mulch.etymology: Probably from Middle English *melsche*, *molsh* (“soft”), from Old English *melsċ*, *milisċ* (“mellow; mild; sweet”), probably from Proto-Germanic **mili* (“honey”).

senses.definition: The generally sterile male or female hybrid offspring of a male donkey and a female horse.
The generally sterile hybrid offspring of any two species of animals.
A stubborn person.
A person paid to smuggle drugs.
senses.example: Police say the young man was only a mule, hired to carry the cocaine across the border.

senses.definition: A coin or medal minted with obverse and reverse designs not normally seen on the same piece, either intentionally or in error.
senses.example: Collectors prize the mule because its obverse and reverse come from two different dies.

senses.definition: A MMORPG character, or NPC companion in a tabletop RPG, used mainly to store extra inventory for the owner's primary character.
senses.example: I parked my mule character in the town so my main hero could carry more loot.

senses.definition: Any of a group of cocktails involving ginger ale or ginger beer, citrus juice, and various liquors.
senses.example: At the bar, she ordered a mule with vodka, lime, and spicy ginger beer.

senses.definition: A kind of triangular sail for a yacht.
senses.example: We rigged a mule sail on the yacht to catch the light summer breeze.

senses.definition: A kind of cotton-spinning machine.
senses.example: The old mill still ran a mule to spin cotton into fine yarn for the local weavers.

senses.definition: Any shoe with an upper covering the front of the foot but without a back flap or strap, leaving the heel exposed.
senses.example: She wore backless mules to the office, which she found easier than heeled pumps.

senses.definition: (rare) A hybrid plant.
senses.example: Botanists call the sterile orchid a mule, since it results from crossing two species.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To smuggle (illegal drugs).
senses.example: Prosecutors say he used his boat to mule cocaine from the coast to the city.

core.definition: A sterile hybrid animal, usually from a male donkey and a female horse, used for carrying loads or riding. Also: a stubborn person.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long u sound that begins with a y glide, like the word mule itself, so do not say it like mewl. Keep the l light and clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the animal. Negative when used for a stubborn person, where it implies someone refuses to move or listen.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mule for the animal mainly in rural, ranch, or hiking contexts, such as mule trips into the Grand Canyon. Calling a person a mule is informal and mildly insulting, so say it with care. The verb sense (to smuggle drugs) is slang used mostly in news and crime contexts.

distinctions.note: A donkey is a separate species, while a mule is a hybrid of a donkey and a horse, so mules are usually bigger and stronger than donkeys.
Stubborn is a general word for refusing to change your mind, while calling someone a mule is more informal and emphasizes that stubbornness.

examples.everyday: We rode mules down into the canyon on our vacation, and my back still hurts.
examples.professional: Don't be a mule about the deadline; let's talk through what we can cut from the scope.
examples.analytical: Scripture warns against behaving like a mule, unreasoning and unresponsive to guidance, which is a helpful image for dogmatic refusal to consider evidence.

nuance.analogy: A mule is like a sturdy but stubborn helper: it does the hard work reliably, yet it will not budge if it decides not to.
nuance.etymology: From Old English mūl, from Latin mulus (mule).
common_mistakes: Saying the word like mewl or mool instead of MYOOL.
Using mule as a casual insult for a friend without considering how it sounds; say stubborn or set in your ways if you want to be gentler.
Confusing the verb sense (to smuggle drugs) with the animal sense in conversation.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible the mule (Hebrew peredh) is a riding and work animal of royalty and the wealthy. In 2 Samuel 13 the fleeing sons of King David mount their mules, and in 1 Kings 1 King Solomon rides on the king's mule to be anointed. In Psalm 32 the psalmist warns the reader not to be like the horse or the mule, which have no understanding and must be controlled by bit and bridle.

mule.etymology: Middle English *mule*, from Anglo-Norman *mule* (“she-mule”) and Old English *mūl*, both ultimately from Latin *mūlus*, from Proto-Indo-European **mukslós*.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being mulish.
senses.example: Her mulishness at the negotiating table frustrated everyone and stalled the deal.

core.definition: The quality of being stubbornly unwilling to change one's mind or to cooperate, even when reason says otherwise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the final -ness be a weak, reduced vowel, close to 'nus'. Do not pronounce the 'i' in the middle as a long 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names an unpleasant trait, usually impatient or pig-headed stubbornness.
nuance.usage_note: This is a literary or descriptive word, not a common spoken term. Americans are more likely to say stubbornness, obstinacy, or being hardheaded in ordinary conversation. Use mulishness in essays, reviews, or when you want a sharper picture of unreasoning refusal.

distinctions.note: Stubbornness is the everyday word and can be neutral or even admirable when it means firm principle. Mulishness is always negative, suggesting obstinacy without good reason.
Obstinacy is more formal and can describe fixed opinions or a long-held refusal. Mulishness adds a sense of animal-like immovability.

examples.professional: His mulishness in code reviews slowed the team down, since he rejected every suggestion without testing it.
examples.analytical: Mulishness is less a failure of argument than a refusal to let argument move the will, and that refusal is what makes it a vice.

nuance.analogy: It is like a mule that stops in the middle of the trail. Logic, a carrot, or a shove cannot make it go forward.
nuance.etymology: From mulish (from mule, plus -ish) plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with stubbornness in positive contexts; mulishness is always a criticism.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable with a long vowel as in 'mew-LISH-ness'.

senses.definition: The quality of being multivalent.

core.definition: The property of having more than one binding site or attachment point, so an object can connect to several targets at once.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MUL, and a lighter secondary stress on -vay-. The ending -lence is pronounced like 'lunss,' with a short, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise scientific or academic term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in chemistry, biology, immunology, and philosophy of language, mostly in writing and lectures. In a general conversation, a native speaker would more likely say 'it can bind to several things' or 'it has multiple binding sites.' The noun form is less common than the adjective 'multivalent.'

distinctions.note: Valence is the general concept of combining power, while multivalence specifically means having several such sites or bonds.
Multivalence is the quality, while multivalent is the adjective describing an object that has it.

examples.everyday: My doctor explained that the flu shot's multivalence means it protects against several strains at once.
examples.professional: The multivalence of the vaccine candidate lets us combine four antigens into a single dose.
examples.analytical: Her argument rests on the multivalence of certain concepts, which resist a single fixed meaning.

nuance.analogy: Multivalence is like a power strip with several outlets: one plug can connect to many devices at the same time.
nuance.etymology: From multi- and valence, from Latin valentia, 'strength,' from valere, 'to be strong.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'vah' instead of 'vay,' which changes the vowel sound.
Using it as a general word for 'variety' or 'diversity' instead of a specific term for binding sites.

senses.definition: Hard to see through, as a fog or mist.
Dark, dim, gloomy.
Cloudy, indistinct, obscure.
senses.example: murky waters

senses.definition: Dishonest, shady.
senses.example: The murky dealings of the city council drew a federal investigation.

core.definition: Dark, dim, and hard to see through, such as fog, dirty water, or a gloomy place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel is the r-colored sound of 'bird', not 'moo'. Say it with a clear American r.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests dirt, confusion, or something hidden, and it can describe water, weather, or a situation with unclear motives.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use murky for water that is muddy, for weather that is dim and foggy, and for situations that are unclear or possibly shady, such as a murky past or murky legal details. In casual speech people often say cloudy or fuzzy for less dramatic cases. It is not rude, but it sounds descriptive and a bit dramatic when used for everyday things.

distinctions.note: Cloudy describes something that is not clear, such as liquid or sky. Murky adds darkness or the sense that you cannot see into it.
Vague describes unclear ideas or language. Murky can describe both physical water and unclear situations.

examples.everyday: The lake was so murky after the storm that we could not see our feet.
examples.professional: The project history is murky, so let's get the original requirements before we make any decisions.
examples.analytical: Her account of the events is murky, and the sources do not clearly establish who made the decision.

nuance.analogy: Like looking into a pond after someone has stirred up the mud.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English mirky, from Old English mirce, meaning dark.
common_mistakes: Saying the vowel like 'oo' (MOO-kee) instead of the r-colored sound of 'bird'.
Misspelling it as murkey.

senses.definition: Synonym of musculature.
senses.example: The muscularity in his forearm was visible as he flexed his fingers.

senses.definition: The degree to which the muscles in a body part are developed.
senses.example: Focussed exercise brought out the muscularity in her calves.

senses.definition: The use of strength.
senses.example: The coach admired the muscularity of the defense, which shoved every attacker off the ball.

core.definition: The degree to which the muscles of the body are developed, or the quality of being strong and physically powerful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, LAIR, which is the stressed syllable of the word. The a is a clear 'air' sound followed by reduced vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it is clinical when describing bodies and more loaded when describing a style, culture or ideal of strength.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use muscularity mostly in written or academic contexts, such as sports science, fitness writing or cultural history. In everyday talk they would more often say 'how muscular he is' or 'his build'. The phrase 'Muscular Christianity' is a historical term for a 19th-century movement that linked faith with physical strength.

distinctions.note: Musculature refers to the arrangement or system of muscles in a body or part; muscularity refers to how developed or strong those muscles are.
Strength is the general capacity to exert force; muscularity focuses on the visible size and development of the muscles.

examples.everyday: After a year of training, his muscularity was obvious to everyone at the gym.
examples.professional: The study measured muscularity in the arms and legs before and after the six-week strength program.
examples.analytical: The muscularity of 19th-century Christian rhetoric reflected anxieties about manhood and national character.

nuance.analogy: Muscularity is the 'size and fitness' of a tool: a well-forged blade is measured not only by its shape but by how dense and strong its metal is.
nuance.etymology: From muscular plus the suffix -ity, from Latin musculus and -itas.
common_mistakes: Using muscularity as a synonym for musculature; they differ in meaning.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in mus-kyuh-LAR-ih-tee.
Confusing muscularity with the adjective muscular in a sentence that needs a noun.

senses.definition: A person who prepares an initiate for entry into a mystery cult, or who teaches mystical doctrines.

core.definition: A person who initiates others into religious mysteries or teaches mystical doctrines to those newly admitted to a sacred group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MIS. The middle 'tuh' is reduced, and the final 'gog' has an open American 'ah' vowel, so it rhymes with 'log'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative when describing secretive or manipulative leaders; neutral when describing a teacher of sacred mysteries.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mystagogue mainly in academic, theological and literary writing about ancient religions, cults and esoteric movements. In everyday speech it sounds very formal or exaggerated. A teacher who initiates people into a movement is often called a guru or spiritual leader in casual American English.

distinctions.note: A mystic seeks or experiences direct union with the divine, while a mystagogue is a teacher who leads others into the mysteries.
Guru is a common American word for a spiritual teacher, while mystagogue is formal and suggests initiation into secret rites.

examples.everyday: My cousin got really into some group where a self-described mystagogue leads the weekend retreats.
examples.professional: The conference paper examined how the mystagogue shaped membership and secrecy in the early cult.
examples.analytical: Plato's portrayal of the poets often resembles that of a mystagogue who promises initiates a privileged vision of truth.

nuance.analogy: A mystagogue is like a tour guide who holds the only key to a locked room, opening it only for those who have been admitted.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mystagōgos, 'one who leads into the mysteries', from mystēs, 'initiate', and agōgos, 'leader'.
common_mistakes: Using mystagogue as a casual word for any teacher, which sounds unnatural.
Pronouncing the final syllable with a long 'oh' sound as 'gohg' rather than 'gog'.

senses.definition: A traditional story which embodies a belief regarding some fact or phenomenon of experience, and in which often the forces of nature and of the soul are personified; a sacred narrative regarding a god, a hero, the origin of the world or of a people, etc.
senses.example: The ancient myth told how the god Prometheus stole fire from the heavens for humanity.

senses.definition: Such stories as a genre.
senses.example: Myth was the product of man's emotion and imagination, acted upon by his surroundings. (E. Clodd, Myths & Dreams (1885), 7, cited after OED)

senses.definition: A commonly-held but false belief, a common misconception; a fictitious or imaginary person or thing; a popular conception about a real person or event which exaggerates or idealizes reality.
senses.example: Scientists debunk the myth that gum stays in the human stomach for seven years.

senses.definition: A person or thing held in excessive or quasi-religious awe or admiration based on popular legend.
senses.example: Father Flanagan was legendary, his institution an American myth. (Tucson (Arizona) Citizen, 20 September 1979, 5A/3, cited after OED)

senses.definition: A person or thing existing only in imagination, or whose actual existence is not verifiable.
senses.example: For years, the rumored lake monster was a myth that nobody could ever prove.

senses.definition: An invented story, theory, or concept.
senses.example: His story is a pure myth.

core.definition: A widely repeated belief that is false, or a traditional story about gods, heroes, or the origins of the world.

pronunciation.tip: End with a voiceless th, placing the tongue lightly between the teeth and blowing air, not a voiced 'th' like in 'this'. Do not add a vowel and say 'my-thuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the sense of traditional stories; negative when used to say an idea is false, as in 'a diet myth'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use myth often in everyday talk to correct a belief, as in 'the idea that cracking knuckles causes arthritis is a myth'. In academic or religious settings it can mean a sacred traditional story, but calling a Bible story a myth may offend religious listeners, so choose your words carefully.

distinctions.note: A legend is a story about a historical figure that has grown with retelling; a myth is a traditional story about gods, origins, or a worldview.
A misconception is an honest error; a myth is a belief repeated so widely that people treat it as true.
A fable is a short story with a moral, often featuring animals; a myth explains origins, gods, or the nature of the world.

examples.everyday: People say you need eight glasses of water a day, but that's really just a myth.
examples.professional: The idea that Agile means no planning is a myth, and our onboarding guide should say so.
examples.analytical: Many scholars read the Gilgamesh flood story as a myth that expresses cultural anxieties rather than a literal chronicle.

nuance.analogy: A myth is like a rumor that has been repeated so often it sounds like history.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mythos, meaning word, speech, or story.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the plural myths with a final /ðz/ instead of /θs/.
Using myth as a synonym for mistake; a myth is a widely repeated belief, not an individual error.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is mythos, meaning a story or account, and the New Testament uses it for stories that are false, empty, or unhelpful to faith. In 1 Timothy 1:4, the reader is told not to occupy themselves with myths and endless genealogies. In 2 Timothy 4:4, people turn away from the truth and wander off into myths. In 2 Peter 1:16, the writer says the apostles did not follow cleverly devised myths.

myth.etymology: From Ancient Greek *μῦθος* (“word, humour, companion, speech, account, rumour, fable”).

senses.definition: Existing in myth.
senses.example: mythical creature

senses.definition: Not real; false or fabricated.
senses.example: Her claim of a secret inheritance was mythical, and the lawyer quickly proved it false.

senses.definition: Very rare.
senses.example: Honest mechanics are almost mythical these days, at least in my neighborhood.

core.definition: Existing only in myth or legend, or not real. Used for creatures, heroes, or events that are imagined or believed without evidence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MITH. The th is voiceless, so place the tongue between the teeth and blow air. The last syllable is reduced to kul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing legends, negative when used to mean something people wrongly believe is real
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mythical for creatures like dragons or heroes from legend, and also for things people believe in without evidence, such as a mythical perfect work-life balance. The second meaning sounds a bit skeptical. In serious writing, people often prefer legendary for heroic stories.

distinctions.note: Mythical describes something that exists in myth or is not real, while mythological refers to the study or body of myths.
Legendary means famous or celebrated, and can be positive, while mythical focuses on being imagined or not real.

examples.everyday: My son is convinced that a mythical dragon lives in the lake behind our house.
examples.professional: The idea that our tests will be perfectly stable is mythical, so we should plan for flaky results.
examples.analytical: Scholars argue that the mythical founder of the city was constructed to explain its political order.

nuance.analogy: A mythical figure is like a map of a country that exists only in a storybook: detailed and beloved, but not on the real ground.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin mythicus, from Greek mythikos, from mythos, story or word.
common_mistakes: Confusing mythical with mythological, which refers to the study or body of myths.
Mispronouncing the th as a d or s sound.

senses.definition: To make more specific.
senses.example: All the food on the menu looked delicious, so I tried to narrow down my choices to only healthy foods.

core.definition: To reduce a large set of options to a smaller, more specific set, so you can choose or decide.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word 'down', which is the strongest word in the phrase. The word 'narrow' is lighter, and the r is clearly pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It is positive or neutral when you are making a decision, and it sounds natural in both casual and professional talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use narrow down constantly in everyday planning, hiring, shopping and problem solving. A natural reply is 'Sure, let me know which ones you like.' Put the object in the middle when it is a pronoun: 'narrow it down', not 'narrow down it'.

distinctions.note: Choose means to pick one option; narrow down means to shrink the list before you pick.
Limit means to set a boundary or maximum; narrow down focuses on removing options until a smaller set remains.

examples.everyday: Can you help me narrow down the restaurant choices? I'm too hungry to decide.
examples.professional: Let's narrow down the candidates to three before the final interviews on Thursday.
examples.analytical: The philosopher narrows the question down to whether moral obligation requires free consent.

nuance.analogy: Narrowing down is like using a sieve: each pass lets through only the pieces that fit your purpose.
nuance.etymology: Narrow from Old English nearu; down from Old English dune, meaning downward.
common_mistakes: Placing a pronoun after down, as in 'narrow down it'; say 'narrow it down'.
Using narrow down for physical shrinking; it usually refers to choices, options or causes.

senses.definition: The state of being naughty.
A naughty act.
senses.example: The toddler's naughtiness was obvious from the crayon marks all over the hallway wall.

core.definition: The quality of behaving badly in a mischievous or playful way, often used for children or for small, harmless misbehavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, NAW. The middle syllable is short and unstressed, so say it quickly, and the final -ness is a reduced 'nus'. Americans often flap the t in naughty so it sounds close to 'NAW-dee'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or affectionate, depending on context. For a child it is gently disapproving; in an adult context it can sound playful or flirtatious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use naughtiness mostly about children, pets, or playful adults, such as 'the kids' naughtiness at bedtime.' For serious wrongdoing, say wrongdoing, misconduct, or wickedness instead. The word is informal enough that it can sound childish in a business or legal setting.

distinctions.note: Mischief is playful trouble-making that is often deliberate and fun, while naughtiness is a broader word for not behaving well.
Wickedness is a strong, morally serious word for evil conduct, far stronger than naughtiness.

examples.everyday: The kids were full of naughtiness at the birthday party, so we had to split them up.
examples.professional: We don't need to treat a late-night prank in the office as anything more than naughtiness.
examples.analytical: Augustine distinguishes the naughtiness of a child's small sins from the deliberate malice of adult wrongdoing.

nuance.analogy: Naughtiness is like the sparkle in a puppy's eyes just before it chews your shoe: mischievous, not malicious.
nuance.etymology: From naughty, which comes from naught (nothing, worthless), plus the suffix -ness; naughty originally meant worthless, then wicked, then mischievous.
common_mistakes: Using naughtiness for serious crime; use wrongdoing or misconduct instead.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'tee'; it is short and quick.

senses.definition: Causing nausea; sickening or disgusting.
senses.example: The smell of the rotting fish was so nauseous that we had to leave the market.

senses.definition: Afflicted with nausea; sick.
senses.example: After the rough boat ride, I felt nauseous and sat down on the dock.

core.definition: Feeling sick to your stomach, as if you might vomit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NAW. The ending -eous is usually pronounced 'shus' in American speech, though 'NAW-zee-us' is also heard and accepted. Keep the first vowel as the open 'aw' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a physical sensation, so it is used about yourself or someone else who feels ill.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, nauseous is widely used to mean 'feeling sick to your stomach,' as in 'I feel nauseous after that ride.' Some traditional grammarians prefer nauseated for the feeling, and nauseous for something that causes it. In formal or medical writing, nauseated is safer. Be careful: nauseating means 'causing nausea,' so a nauseating smell is disgusting.

distinctions.note: Nauseated is the more formal and precise word for the feeling; nauseous is common in everyday American speech for the same meaning.
Nauseating means causing nausea or disgust, so it describes the thing, not the person who feels it.

examples.everyday: I feel a little nauseous after that long drive, so let's stop for a snack.
examples.professional: If you feel nauseous during the video call, just step away and let me know.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers have called the crowd's cruelty nauseous, though the word describes a bodily reaction rather than a moral judgment.

nuance.analogy: Feeling nauseous is like a boat rocking in your stomach: you are not sick yet, but the motion warns you that you might be.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nauseosus, from nausea, from Greek naus (ship).
common_mistakes: Confusing nauseous (I feel sick) with nauseating (it makes me sick).
Using nauseous with a strong, disgusted sense in formal writing; choose disgusted or repulsed instead.

nauseous.etymology: From Latin *nauseōsus* (“causing nausea”), corresponding synchronically to *nausea* + *-ous*.

conversation.text: I feel a little nauseous after that roller coaster.
Long car rides make me nauseous if I read.
She was nauseous all morning, so she skipped breakfast.

senses.definition: A long, thin, sharp implement usually for piercing as in sewing, embroidery, acupuncture, tattooing, body piercing, medical injections, sutures, etc; or a blunt but otherwise similar implement used for forming loops or knots in crafts such as darning, knitting, tatting, etc.
senses.example: The seamstress threaded the needle to sew on a button.

senses.definition: Any slender, pointed object resembling a needle, such as a pointed crystal, a sharp pinnacle of rock, an obelisk, etc.
senses.example: The climbers paused beneath a towering needle of granite that rose sharply above the valley.

senses.definition: A fine measurement indicator on a dial or graph.
senses.example: a compass needle

senses.definition: A sensor for playing phonograph records, a phonograph stylus.
senses.example: Ziggy bought some diamond needles for his hi-fi phonograph.

senses.definition: A needle-like leaf found on some conifers.
senses.example: In winter, the spruce dropped every dry needle onto the frozen trail behind our cabin.

senses.definition: A strong beam resting on props, used as a temporary support during building repairs.
senses.example: The contractor installed a heavy needle under the wall to hold up the floor while repairing the foundation.

senses.definition: The death penalty carried out by lethal injection.
senses.example: The governor refused to sign the order that would send the prisoner to the needle.

senses.definition: A text string that is searched for within another string. (see: needle in a haystack)
senses.example: Our search function scans every log file for the needle, the exact error string.

senses.definition: A move in which the performer begins with two hands and one leg on the floor, then kicks the other leg into a full split.
senses.example: She finished her floor routine with a daring needle, dropping straight into a full split.

senses.definition: Any of various species of damselfly of the genus Synlestes, endemic to Australia.
senses.example: Entomologists in Queensland spotted a rare needle hovering over the creek, a species found nowhere else.

senses.definition: To pierce with a needle, especially for sewing or acupuncture.
senses.example: The nurse needled the vein carefully, so the patient barely felt the sharp pinch.

senses.definition: To tease in order to provoke; to poke fun at.
senses.example: Billy needled his sister incessantly about her pimples.

senses.definition: To form, or be formed, in the shape of a needle.
senses.example: to needle crystals

core.definition: A long, thin, sharp metal tool with an eye at one end, used for sewing and knitting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced syllabic l with no vowel sound, so it sounds like 'NEE-dl'. Avoid adding an 'uh' sound at the end. Stress does not shift in the verb form.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a common, everyday object word with no emotional charge as a noun. As a verb meaning to tease, it is mildly negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'needle' constantly for sewing, knitting, shots at the doctor's office, and the pine needles of trees. Note that 'pine needle' is one word in the sense of leaves, and 'needle' for a shot is common in both casual and medical talk. As a verb meaning to tease, it is informal and friendly among friends but can irritate if repeated.

distinctions.note: A pin is usually shorter, thicker and has a round head, while a needle is longer, thinner and has an eye for thread.
Thread is the material that goes through the eye of the needle; the two are used together but are different objects.

examples.everyday: Can you hand me a needle and some thread so I can fix this button on my shirt?
examples.professional: The nurse said the flu shot needle is very small, so most people barely feel it.
examples.analytical: In Matthew 19:24 Jesus uses the image of a camel passing through the eye of a needle to describe the difficulty a rich person faces entering the kingdom of God.

nuance.analogy: A needle is like a very thin zipper pull on a sewing journey: it carries the thread through the cloth, step by step.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'nǣdl', related to 'nǣdl' and 'needle' in Germanic languages, meaning a sewing needle.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun 'needle' with the verb 'to needle' in casual talk; the verb means to tease, not to sew.
Saying 'a needle of pine' instead of 'a pine needle'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Matthew 19:24 (RSV), Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. The Greek word is 'rhaphis' (ῥαφίς), meaning a sewing needle. The image is a deliberate exaggeration that shows how hard it is for a person who trusts in riches to enter God's kingdom. Parallel passages are Mark 10:25 and Luke 18:25.

needle.etymology: From Middle English *nedle*, from Old English *nǣdl*, from **nāþlu*, from Proto-Germanic **nēþlō*, from pre-Germanic **neh₁-tleh₂*, from Proto-Indo-European **neh₁-* (“to spin, twist”).

senses.definition: Not needed; unnecessary.
senses.example: This new project of yours will only be a needless expense.

senses.definition: Needlessly, without cause.
senses.example: She apologized needlessly for a mistake that nobody had even noticed.

core.definition: Not necessary; done or existing without any good reason or purpose.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable; the middle syllable is a syllabic l, and the final 'less' is a reduced 'ləs' that sounds like 'lis'. Don't pronounce it as 'NEED-lehss'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly critical; it suggests something was unnecessary, wasteful, or caused trouble for no reason.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'needless' often in phrases such as 'needless to say' and 'needless worry', and it is common in everyday talk and writing. 'Needless to say' is a polite way to introduce something obvious, and it is followed by a sentence. Saying 'needless to say' before a statement is natural and not rude.

distinctions.note: 'Unnecessary' is the more general word and can sound neutral, while 'needless' often implies waste or that the thing caused a problem.
'Useless' means having no value at all, while 'needless' only means not required, which may still be useful in another way.

examples.everyday: Needless to say, the restaurant was packed on Friday night, so we waited an hour for a table.
examples.professional: Let's avoid needless meetings this week, since most of the decisions can be made by email.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the policy adds needless complexity without improving outcomes for the people it claims to help.

nuance.analogy: A needless step is like walking to the far end of a parking lot when you could have parked right next to the door.
nuance.etymology: From 'need' plus the suffix '-less', meaning without need.
common_mistakes: Using 'needless' as a synonym for 'needed'; the two words have opposite meanings.
Writing 'needless to say' with a comma after 'say' when it is followed by a clause; the usual form is 'Needless to say, ...' with a comma after 'say'.

senses.definition: Recently made, or created.
senses.example: This is a new scratch on my car! The band just released a new album.

senses.definition: Of recent origin; having taken place recently.
senses.example: I can't see you for a while; the pain is still too new. Did you see the new King Lear at the theater?

senses.definition: Additional; recently discovered.
senses.example: We turned up some new evidence from the old files.

senses.definition: Current or later, as opposed to former.
senses.example: My new car is much better than my previous one, even though it is older. We had been in our new house for five years by then.

senses.definition: Used to distinguish something established more recently, named after something or some place previously existing.
senses.example: New Bond Street is an extension of Bond Street.

senses.definition: In original condition; pristine; not previously worn or used.
senses.example: Are you going to buy a new car or a second-hand one?

senses.definition: Refreshed, reinvigorated, reformed.
senses.example: That shirt is dirty. Go and put on a new one. I feel like a new person after a good night's sleep. After the accident, I saw the world with new eyes.

senses.definition: Newborn.
senses.example: My sister has a new baby, and our mother is excited to finally have a grandchild.

senses.definition: Strange, unfamiliar or not previously known.
senses.example: The idea was new to me. I need to meet new people.

senses.definition: Recently arrived or appeared.
senses.example: Have you met the new guy in town? He is the new kid at school.

senses.definition: Inexperienced or unaccustomed at some task.
senses.example: Don't worry that you're new at this job; you'll get better with time. I'm new at this business, I'm still new to the work.

senses.definition: Of a period of time, next; about to begin or recently begun.
senses.example: We expect to grow at 10% annually in the new decade.

senses.definition: Synonym of newly, especially in composition.
senses.example: new-born, new-formed, new-found, new-mown hay, new-laid eggs

senses.definition: As new; from scratch.
senses.example: They are scraping the site clean to build new.

senses.definition: Things that are new.
senses.example: Out with the old, in with the new.

senses.definition: A typically light-colored lager brewed by the bottom-fermentation method.
senses.example: The bartender suggested a cold new instead of the heavy stout we had ordered.

senses.definition: Synonym of new up.
senses.example: In the constructor, the class will new up a fresh database connection each time.

core.definition: Recently made, created, or discovered; not old, used, or existing before.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long oo sound. Many Americans say it without a y sound, though nyoo is also heard, so do not add a schwa or an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. New usually sounds appealing in ads and conversation, though it can also mean unfamiliar, which is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use new constantly, at home and at work (Did you see the new menu? I'm new here). Saying I'm new to this is a polite way to ask for help, and it is never rude. In formal writing, recent or novel may fit better in some contexts.

distinctions.note: Novel stresses that something is original or unlike anything before; new only says it is recent or first.
Recent refers to time only and sounds more formal; new can also mean different from what came before.
Fresh suggests clean or not stale, often about food; new is about when something was made or started.

examples.everyday: Hey, did you try the new coffee shop on Main Street?
examples.professional: We're launching a new dashboard for the sales team next Monday.
examples.analytical: A new theory must explain the old data as well as the anomalies that the old theory could not.

nuance.analogy: Like a page that has just been printed: nothing has been written on it yet, so it is blank and ready.
nuance.etymology: From Old English nīwe, from Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, from the Indo-European root *néwos.
common_mistakes: Saying I am new of the city instead of new to the city or new in the city.
Confusing new with news in speech; the words sound similar but news is a different word.

new.etymology: From Middle English *neowe*, *neue*, *new*, *newe*, *nywe*, from Old English *nēowe*, *nīewe*, *nīowe*, *nīwe*, from **niwi*, from Proto-Germanic **niwjaz* (“new”), from Proto-Indo-European **néwos*, **néwyos* (“new”).

senses.definition: A period covering the first few days of a calendar year.
senses.example: We never go away at the New Year because on New Year’s Day the whole family gets together.

senses.definition: In particular, January 1 in the Julian and Gregorian calendar (New Year’s Day) and the days following.

core.definition: The first days of the calendar year, especially January 1 and the days just after it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress New more than Year, and pronounce the r clearly at the end of Year. Do not add an extra vowel before the r.

nuance.connotation: Positive; associated with hope, fresh starts and celebration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say New Year for both the holiday period and the start of the calendar year. Happy New Year is the standard greeting from January 1 through the first week or so, and a natural reply is Happy New Year to you too. The holiday itself is usually called New Year's, with an apostrophe.

distinctions.note: New Year's Day is specifically January 1, while New Year can refer to the wider period around it.
Lunar New Year follows the lunar calendar and falls in January or February; New Year alone usually means January 1 in American contexts.

examples.everyday: Happy New Year! Are you doing anything special this year?
examples.professional: Let's set our quarterly goals early in the New Year so we can start strong in January.
examples.analytical: Many cultures mark the New Year at different points, which shows that the calendar is a human convention rather than a natural fact.

nuance.analogy: A New Year is like a clean page in a notebook: the old entries are still there, but you start writing on a fresh line.
nuance.etymology: From new plus Old English gēar, year.
common_mistakes: Writing New Years without an apostrophe in the holiday names, where New Year's is standard.
Saying in the New Year when you mean on New Year's Day for a specific date.

core.definition: A Pharisee and member of the Jewish council who visited Jesus secretly at night and later helped bury him.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the third syllable, 'dee.' The last syllable is a reduced 'mus,' not 'mes'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the name is respectful in Christian contexts, describing a sincere but cautious seeker.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the name mainly in churches, Bible studies and religious conversations. The name is often used to describe someone who comes to faith or questions quietly, sometimes called a 'Nicodemus' figure. Pronounce the name naturally in English; it is not a common everyday word.

examples.everyday: My friend says her grandfather was a bit of a Nicodemus, quietly reading the Bible long before he told anyone.
examples.professional: In this sermon series we will look at Nicodemus and what his night visit teaches about seeking faith.
examples.analytical: The Gospel of John presents Nicodemus as a figure whose hesitant approach to Jesus illuminates the tension between secret belief and public confession.

nuance.analogy: Nicodemus is like someone who slips into a meeting after dark to ask a question he is afraid to raise in daylight.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'Nikodemos,' combining 'nike' (victory) and 'demos' (people).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable instead of the 'dee' syllable.
Confusing him with Nicolas, the deacon named in Acts 6:5.
nuance.biblical_note: Nicodemus appears in the Gospel of John. He is a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews who visits Jesus at night and hears the teaching about being born from above. In John 7:50-52 he speaks up cautiously in the council, and in John 19:39-42 he brings a large quantity of myrrh and aloes for Jesus's burial. Together these passages show a man who moves from secret curiosity toward open loyalty.

senses.definition: One who niggles; a constant critic.

core.definition: A person who constantly complains about or criticizes small details, often in a petty and tiresome way.

pronunciation.tip: It has two syllables with stress on the first, and the final syllable is a reduced vowel like the -er in 'butter' with a flapped feel. Note that niggle is a verb with the same stress.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes someone who makes minor complaints that annoy others.
nuance.usage_note: Niggler is rare and literary, and most Americans would say nitpicker, fusspot, or perfectionist. Some listeners hear the sound of a racial slur in the word, so it is best to avoid it in conversation. Use it, if at all, in writing when you want a precise word for a habitual minor critic.

distinctions.note: Nitpicker is the common American word for someone who points out tiny flaws; use it in speech instead.
A critic judges work seriously, while a niggler focuses on trivial points that do not matter much.

examples.professional: Our reviewer flags every comma and footnote, which slows the whole document down.
examples.analytical: Every committee has its niggler, whose objections are rarely wrong but are seldom decisive for the outcome.

nuance.analogy: A niggler is like a gnat that keeps circling your head: tiny, persistent, and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From niggle, a verb meaning to fuss over trifles; the origin of niggle is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using niggler in speech where nitpicker is far more natural.
Confusing niggler with niggard, which means stingy, not a petty critic.

senses.definition: The nipple (noun sense 1) and the areola together.
senses.example: The dermatologist examined the nipple and areola for any scaling or unusual color changes.

senses.definition: A mechanical device through which liquids or gases can be passed in a regulated manner.
senses.example: The hydroponic system uses a nipple to deliver nutrient solution to each plant at a steady rate.

senses.definition: An artificial nipple (noun sense 1) used for bottle-feeding infants.
senses.example: We bought three bottles and a box of silicone nipples before our daughter came home from the hospital.

senses.definition: Any small physical protrusion, such as the lumps on the F and J keys on computer keyboards.
senses.example: The tactile nipple on the J key helps me find my home row without looking at the keyboard.

senses.definition: Any small physical protrusion on an automotive, a machine part or any other part that fits into a groove on another part.
senses.example: The bracket's small nipple slides into the groove on the frame, locking the two pieces together.

senses.definition: A short tube threaded at both ends, used as a connector.
senses.example: The plumber used a brass nipple to connect the two pipe fittings without leaking.

senses.definition: An internally threaded piece which holds a bicycle spoke in place on the rim.
senses.example: Turn the nipples on to the bicycle spokes only one turn, for each spoke on the new wheel all the way around until they are all snug, then check alignment.

senses.definition: A pointing stick.
senses.example: On the old laptop, I moved the cursor with the red nipple in the middle of the keyboard.

senses.definition: The projection of a mammary gland from which, on female therian mammals, milk is secreted.
senses.example: The mammal's nipple is the site where milk flows to the young during nursing.

senses.definition: (historical) A perforated segment that fits into part of the breech of a muzzle-loading gun, on which the percussion cap is fixed.
senses.example: The rusty nipple on the antique musket was still fitted with a cracked percussion cap.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To fit (a baby's bottle, etc.) with a nipple.
senses.example: The machinist nippled the new brass fitting so the water line could attach securely.

senses.definition: To give one's nipple to (a baby) to allow breastfeeding.
senses.example: For the first month, she nipples the baby every two hours while learning to nurse.

core.definition: A rubber or silicone cap on a baby's bottle, through which the baby sucks milk or formula.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NIP. The second syllable is a reduced 'uhl', with a light l, not a full 'ell' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the baby-bottle sense. The word can carry an intimate or sexual sense in other contexts, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nipple' for the rubber part of a baby bottle, where British speakers often say 'teat'. Parents say 'Do you have a spare nipple?' or 'Get a new nipple for the bottle'. In general conversation, it is best to say 'bottle nipple' or 'baby bottle nipple' to avoid confusion.

distinctions.note: Americans use 'teat' mainly for animals' milk-producing parts and seldom for baby bottles. For a bottle, 'nipple' is the standard American word.
A pacifier is a soother for babies to suck on; a nipple is the rubber part on a bottle that delivers milk or formula.

examples.everyday: This bottle is leaking, so we need a new nipple from the store.
examples.professional: The nipple flow rate is listed on the package, so check that it matches the feeding stage for infants.
examples.analytical: Feeding researchers often compare how the shape of a nipple affects the infant's suck and milk intake.

nuance.analogy: Like the cap on a water bottle that lets you drink, the nipple is the small rubber part that lets the baby drink.
common_mistakes: Using 'teat' for a baby bottle, which sounds unusual to Americans.
Stressing the second syllable, as in nip-PUHL.

nipple.etymology: From earlier *neple*, *nypil*, *neble*, believed to be a diminutive of *nib*, *neb* (“tip, point”), equivalent to *nib* + *le*.

senses.definition: A knot, knob, protuberance or swelling.
senses.example: The doctor felt a hard node in her neck and ordered a scan.

senses.definition: A computer or other device attached to a network.
senses.example: If one node fails, the rest of the network keeps running normally.

senses.definition: The point at which the lines of a funicular machine meet from different angular directions.
senses.example: The engineers checked every node where the cables met in the funicular's frame.

senses.definition: The point at which a curve crosses itself, being a double point of the curve. See crunode and acnode.
senses.example: The cubic curve has a node at the origin where it crosses itself.

senses.definition: A similar point on a surface, where there is more than one tangent-plane.
senses.example: The cone's vertex is a node of the surface where several tangent planes meet.

senses.definition: A vertex or a leaf in a graph of a network, or other element in a data structure.
A hole in the gnomon of a sundial, through which passes the ray of light which marks the hour of the day, the parallels of the Sun's declination, its place in the ecliptic, etc.
senses.example: The sundial's gnomon has a small node that casts a sharp spot of light.

senses.definition: The word of interest in a KWIC, surrounded by left and right cotexts.
senses.example: In the concordance, each node appears centered between its left and right cotexts.

senses.definition: A region of an electric circuit connected only by (ideal) wires (i.e. the voltage between any two points on the same node must be zero).
senses.example: Kirchhoff's current law applies at every node where three wires meet.

senses.definition: A point in a parse tree that can be assigned a syntactic category label.
senses.example: Each word in the sentence is attached to a node labeled with its part of speech.

senses.definition: The point where the orbit of a planet, as viewed from the Sun, intersects the ecliptic. The ascending and descending nodes refer respectively to the points where the planet moves from South to North and N to S; their respective symbols are ☊ and ☋.
senses.example: The comet crosses the ecliptic at a node, where its orbit intersects the plane.

senses.definition: A leaf node.
senses.example: In a binary tree, every leaf node has no children.

senses.definition: A hard concretion or incrustation which forms upon bones attacked with rheumatism, gout, or syphilis; sometimes also, a swelling in the neighborhood of a joint.
senses.example: Doctors found a bony node on his toe, a sign of advanced gout.

senses.definition: A point along a standing wave where the wave has minimal amplitude.
senses.example: At the node of a standing wave, the string stays motionless while it vibrates.

senses.definition: A point in a cladogram from which two clades branch, representing the presumed ancestor.
senses.example: On the cladogram, the node joins two clades that share a common ancestor.

senses.definition: (rare) The knot, intrigue, or plot of a dramatic work.
senses.example: The novel's node is the moment the conspiracy is finally exposed.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A connection point in a network, graph or data structure, such as a device, a vertex or a branching point.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long 'oh' glide followed by a clear voiced d. Do not say 'not' or 'nut' (the vowel in 'knot' is different in American English).

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American tech and data work, a node is any point in a network, a computer or device connected to others, or a vertex in a graph or tree. In medicine, Americans say 'lymph node' or 'a swollen node', and in everyday life the word mostly comes up in discussions of the network or health. Americans would not normally use 'node' for a knot in a rope, where 'knot' is the usual word.

distinctions.note: In graph theory the two are synonyms, but 'node' is more common in computing and networks, while 'vertex' is typical in pure mathematics.
A node in computing is a connection point. A nodule is a small rounded lump in tissue, and it is a medical term.

examples.everyday: The doctor said the swelling was in a lymph node, which is usually nothing serious.
examples.professional: Each sensor node sends its readings to the cloud every five minutes, so one dead node won't stop the whole system.
examples.analytical: In a decision tree, each internal node tests one feature, and each branch leads to a child node or a final prediction.

nuance.analogy: A node is like a junction on a road map, where several roads meet and traffic can change direction.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nodus, 'knot'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'not' or 'knot' (/nɑt/), which changes the meaning.
Using 'node' for a knot in rope or wood, where Americans say 'knot'.

node.etymology: From Middle English *node*, borrowed from Latin *nōdus*.

senses.definition: The exercise of reason.
senses.example: Plato's dialogues describe philosophers reaching truth through noesis rather than through sensory evidence.

senses.definition: The consciousness component of noetics, which concerns the duality of noesis and noema.
senses.example: The seminar contrasted noesis with noema when discussing how the mind relates to its objects.

senses.definition: Cognition, the functioning of intellect.
senses.example: Her reasoning showed sharp noesis, and she grasped the argument faster than anyone else in the room.

core.definition: In philosophy, the act of knowing or thinking; the mind's active grasp of an object, distinct from the object itself.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, EE, and the final s is a plain s, not a z. Avoid turning the middle into a long a sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It carries no positive or negative charge; it names a concept.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter noesis mainly in philosophy, phenomenology, and Orthodox theology, usually in discussions of Husserl or Patristic thought. It is never used in casual conversation. In academic writing, define it briefly the first time, and use it alongside noema when discussing the act-object relation.

distinctions.note: Noesis is the act of consciousness, while noema is the object as intended by that act.
Reason is the general faculty of thinking; noesis is a narrower term for the intellectual act itself, in phenomenological or classical usage.
Cognition is the broad modern term for mental processes; noesis is a philosophical term with a specific Greek origin.

examples.everyday: I don't think my friend would ever use the word noesis, but she likes to talk about how we know things.
examples.professional: In the workshop paper, we separated the noesis of the user's query from the noema of the retrieved document.
examples.analytical: Husserl argues that every noesis is directed toward a noema, so the act of perceiving a tree cannot be understood apart from the tree as meant.

nuance.analogy: If an object is the photograph, noesis is the camera's act of taking it: the process of capturing, not the picture itself.
nuance.etymology: From Greek noēsis, 'perception, understanding', from noein, 'to perceive, think', from nous, 'mind'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a z sound at the end, as in 'noe-zis'.
Using it as a synonym for knowledge in everyday speech, where it sounds pretentious.

noesis.etymology: Ancient Greek *νόησις* (“concept”, “idea”, “intelligence”, “understanding”), from *νοεῖν* (“to intend”, “to perceive”, “to see”, “to understand”) (from *νοῦς* (“mind”, “thought”), from *νόος*) + *-σις*, suffix forming nouns of action.

senses.definition: In a nominal manner; in name only.
Slightly.
senses.example: The price rose only nominally, a few cents, so nobody complained at the register.

senses.definition: As a noun.

core.definition: In name only; officially or on paper, but not in actual practice or fact.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable NAH. The middle syllables are weak schwas, and the ending is a clear lee sound, not lay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it hints that an official title or status hides the reality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nominally often in news and everyday talk to point out a gap between official status and reality, as in nominally a democracy or nominally in charge. It sounds analytical rather than rude. A natural reply in conversation is 'Right, on paper' or 'In theory, yeah'.

distinctions.note: Officially states that a status is real; nominally suggests the status exists in name only, without real effect.
Technically means strictly by the rules; nominally stresses that the label does not match reality.

examples.everyday: Our landlord is nominally the owner, but his brother handles everything, so call him instead.
examples.professional: Dana is nominally the project lead, but the architecture decisions are really made by the platform team.
examples.analytical: The charter nominally guarantees equal rights, yet its enforcement mechanisms remain largely absent.

nuance.analogy: Like an honorary title on a business card: the words are there, but the real power sits somewhere else.
nuance.etymology: From nominal, from Latin nominalis 'of names', from nomen 'name', plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using nominally to mean mostly or nearly, as in nominally 90% complete; it means in name only, so use it for titles and labels.

senses.definition: A logic that is not classical: one that extends or deviates from classical logic.

core.definition: Any system of logic that departs from classical logic, for example by rejecting bivalence or the law of excluded middle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of classical as KLAS, and LAH in logic, with the vowel of cot. The final -ic is pronounced ik, not ick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in philosophy of logic, mathematics and computer science, often in the plural as non-classical logics. It does not appear in everyday talk. In conversation people name the specific system, such as intuitionistic logic or fuzzy logic.

distinctions.note: Intuitionistic logic is one specific non-classical logic that rejects the law of excluded middle as a general truth; non-classical logic is the whole family.
Fuzzy logic allows degrees of truth; it is one type of non-classical logic, but not all non-classical logics are fuzzy.

examples.everyday: A philosophy major told me non-classical logic lets a sentence be partly true, and I got lost right away.
examples.professional: The formal verification team uses a non-classical logic that handles missing data without forcing every claim to be true or false.
examples.analytical: A non-classical logic extends or rejects the principle of bivalence, so that a proposition need not be simply true or false.

nuance.analogy: Like a traffic system with more than two signals: instead of only red and green, there are yellow and flashing states too.
nuance.etymology: Non- from Latin 'not'; logic from Greek logikē, from logos 'reason, word'.
common_mistakes: Stressing classical on the wrong syllable; say KLAS-ih-kuhl, not klas-SIK-al.
Treating non-classical logic as one specific system; it is a broad family of systems.

senses.definition: The state of being under legal age; minority, the fact of being a minor.

core.definition: The state of being under the legal age of adulthood; minority, or the period of being a minor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and the final 'age' sounds like 'ij', as in 'bridge'. Do not add an extra syllable before the 'j'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; used in legal or literary contexts, sometimes with a sense of youthful immaturity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use nonage in everyday speech. In the United States the usual words are minor, minority, or underage. You may meet nonage in legal writing or older novels.

distinctions.note: Minority is the common American legal and everyday term; nonage is more literary.
Adolescence describes a developmental stage; nonage refers specifically to legal status as a minor.

examples.professional: Because the account holder was still in nonage, the bank required a parent's signature.
examples.analytical: The author treats nonage as a condition of dependence, in which the child cannot yet bind himself by contract.

nuance.analogy: Nonage is like a locked gate: you are on the path to adulthood, but you cannot yet go through it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French nonage, from non- 'not' and age 'age'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'non-AJ', with stress on the second syllable.
Using nonage for everyday youth; in American English 'minor' or 'teenager' is more natural.

senses.definition: Something one likes.
senses.example: Ah, a discussion of definitional minutia: just my cup of tea!

core.definition: Not something one likes or enjoys; not one's kind of thing. The dictionary's 'something one likes' is the opposite of the everyday meaning.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'tea' at the end. 'Of' reduces to a weak 'uhv', and the phrase links smoothly, so 'cup of' sounds like 'cup-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It politely signals dislike without being harsh.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this to decline or distance themselves from an activity, a type of music, or a kind of food, as in 'Opera's not my cup of tea.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, I figured,' or simply asking what they prefer. Do not say 'It's my cup of tea' to mean you dislike something; that means you like it.

distinctions.note: 'Not my thing' is more casual and slightly more common in speech; 'not my cup of tea' sounds a little more old-fashioned and British in origin.
'Not for me' is a plain, direct refusal, while 'not my cup of tea' describes a general lack of taste for something.

collocations: it's not my cup of tea
not really my cup of tea
not quite my cup of tea
that's just not my cup of tea
horror movies are not my cup of tea

examples.everyday: Thanks for the invite, but reality TV is just not my cup of tea.
examples.professional: The team offered a happy hour at the bowling alley, but that's not my cup of tea, so I'll skip it.
examples.analytical: For many readers, the philosophical novel is not their cup of tea, yet its formal experiments reward patience.

nuance.analogy: Like a drink that tastes wrong to you: you can see others enjoying it, but you would never order it yourself.
nuance.etymology: Originated in British English in the late 1800s and spread to American English; the 'cup' image is figurative.
common_mistakes: Saying 'It's my cup of tea' to mean you dislike something, which reverses the meaning.
Changing 'my' to 'your' or 'his' inconsistently; the phrase must match the speaker or subject.

conversation.text: Horror movies are not my cup of tea.
Golf is not really my cup of tea, but I'll come along.
Sales calls are not my cup of tea; I prefer the analysis side.
Spicy food is just not my cup of tea.
Jazz is not my cup of tea, but my wife loves it.

senses.definition: The quality of being obliging; the tendency to cater for the desires of others.

core.definition: The quality of being willing to help or accommodate others; a ready willingness to do what people ask.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BLY, the second syllable. The -ing is a short, reduced 'ing', not 'eeng', and the final -ness is a weak 'nuss'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it describes a helpful, accommodating disposition. It can slightly suggest someone who goes along too easily.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use obligingness mainly in writing or formal description, such as a reference letter praising a colleague's obligingness. In everyday talk they usually say 'she's so helpful' or 'really accommodating.' Calling someone obliging is a compliment, but a person can also be too obliging, meaning they say yes to everything.

distinctions.note: Helpfulness is doing useful things for others; obligingness is a willingness to accommodate requests, often in small matters.
Compliance means following rules or orders, often under pressure; obligingness is voluntary and friendly.

examples.everyday: The front desk clerk's obligingness made our late check-in so much easier.
examples.professional: Her obligingness with other teams kept the cross-department project moving smoothly.
examples.analytical: Aristotle would say such obligingness is a virtue only when it serves a good end rather than mere people-pleasing.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-hung door that swings open at a light push, an obliging person responds readily to what others need.
nuance.etymology: From oblige (from Latin obligare, to bind), with the suffixes -ing and -ness.
common_mistakes: Confusing obligingness with obligation, which means a duty you must perform
Putting the stress on the first syllable (OB-li-jing-ness)

senses.definition: Extremely offensive or unpleasant; very annoying, contemptible, or odious.
senses.example: Throwing stones at the bus is another example of your obnoxious behavior.

senses.definition: Unjustly disagreeable, argumentative or objectionable; brazenly rude.
senses.example: He was an especially obnoxious and detestable specimen of a man.

senses.definition: Causing harm or injury; harmful, hurtful, injurious.
Deserving of blame or punishment; blameworthy, guilty.
Under the authority or power of someone; subject, subordinate; hence, deferential, submissive, subservient.
Followed by to: likely to do something.

core.definition: Very unpleasant, rude or annoying, in a way that makes other people dislike you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NAHK, and the ending -ious is pronounced shus. Americans say the first syllable quickly as uhb, with a weak vowel.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative, describing behavior that is annoying, rude or offensive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use obnoxious in everyday speech to describe people, behavior or noises that are irritating, such as an obnoxious neighbor or obnoxious music. It is fairly strong, so saying someone is obnoxious can be a serious criticism. It is not usually used for mild annoyance; say annoying for that.

distinctions.note: Annoying is mild and common; obnoxious is stronger and suggests the person is rude or offensive.
Offensive focuses on causing hurt or outrage; obnoxious focuses on being irritating and unpleasant to be around.
Rude describes a lack of politeness; obnoxious suggests more aggressive, self-centered behavior.

examples.everyday: The guy in the next apartment plays his music so loud at night that he's become really obnoxious.
examples.professional: Someone in the meeting made obnoxious comments about my model, so I asked the group to focus on the data.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that a debate that rewards obnoxious certainty over careful reasoning distorts public understanding.

nuance.analogy: An obnoxious person is like a car alarm that keeps going off when nobody needs it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obnoxius, exposed to harm, liable, from ob- (before) and noxa (harm).
common_mistakes: Using obnoxious for mild annoyance; annoying is more natural for small irritations.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying ub-NOK-shus.

senses.definition: An exit strategy.
senses.example: Our team's off-ramp is to sell the product to a larger company if funding dries up.

core.definition: A short road that leads vehicles off a highway or freeway to a city street or another road.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'ramp', and 'off' has a lighter secondary stress. Pronounce the 'r' clearly and keep the 'off' vowel short and rounded.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday term used in driving and navigation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'off-ramp' for the road that takes you off a highway, and 'on-ramp' for the road that takes you onto it. People often give directions like 'Take the next off-ramp.' In British English this is called a slip road, so American speakers would not normally use that term. The word is also used figuratively in some business contexts, but the literal meaning is more common.

distinctions.note: Exit can mean any way out, including a highway exit sign; off-ramp is the specific road that leaves the highway.
An on-ramp brings vehicles onto a highway, while an off-ramp takes them off it.

examples.everyday: Take the next off-ramp, and then turn left at the gas station.
examples.professional: The project timeline should have an off-ramp if the vendor misses the first milestone, so we can switch plans without losing the budget.
examples.analytical: Her essay argues that the policy created an off-ramp for corporations, allowing them to escape accountability while appearing compliant.

nuance.analogy: An off-ramp is like a side door off a busy hallway that lets you leave the main flow without stopping everything.
nuance.etymology: From off plus ramp (an inclined road or passage).
common_mistakes: Saying 'exit ramp' as the only term; both are used, but 'off-ramp' is common in American speech.
Using 'off-ramp' for the highway itself or for a city street.
Confusing it with 'on-ramp', which leads onto the highway.

conversation.text: Take the next off-ramp, and we'll find somewhere to eat.
There was a stalled car on the off-ramp.
The hotel is at the bottom of the off-ramp, on the right.

senses.definition: Something which shoots off or separates from a main stem or branch of a plant.
senses.example: the offshoots of a tree

senses.definition: Something which develops from something else.
senses.example: an offshoot of a criminal organization

core.definition: Something that develops from a larger thing, such as a branch of a plant, a company, or an idea.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OFF. The second syllable has the 'oo' vowel of 'boot' and the final t is clear, not silent. Don't say 'shute'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be positive, as in a successful spin-off, or mildly negative, as a minor side branch.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use offshoot for companies, projects, and ideas that grew out of a larger one, as in 'an offshoot of the company.' Spin-off is also common, especially for TV shows and products. Offshoot can sound a bit literary when describing a family line.

distinctions.note: Spin-off is more common for businesses and TV shows, while offshoot is broader and natural for ideas and groups.
A branch is part of a whole, while an offshoot has separated and may develop independently.

examples.everyday: That little coffee shop downtown is an offshoot of the chain across the river.
examples.professional: The security team split off an offshoot project that focuses on identity verification.
examples.analytical: Modern existentialism is an offshoot of earlier debates about human freedom and responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Like a new shoot growing from the side of a tree, still connected to its roots.
nuance.etymology: From off plus shoot, something that shoots off from the main stem.
common_mistakes: Using offshoot as a verb; it is only a noun.
Using it where spin-off is the normal American term for a product or TV series.

senses.definition: A person who is experienced at a certain activity.
senses.example: My tax advisor is an old hand at dealing with auditors.

core.definition: A person who has a lot of practical experience with a particular job, activity or situation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HAND, and old is weaker, so the d links smoothly into the h, giving a sound close to 'ohl-HAND'. Keep the vowel in hand short and open.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's practical skill and experience, and it can be said with respect in workplaces or teams.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use old hand for people who know how a place or system works, such as a longtime employee, a sports veteran or a skilled negotiator.
